Accepted — and the reasoning is the right one: it scores on two of the three v1 tests, and "not perpetually worried about needing to rewrite things" is exactly the kind of ambient anxiety that decides whether you actually live in a tool. Let me record it, because it has three consequences worth having in writing.
**D13** recorded, `features.md` updated. Three consequences of moving branching into v1 that are worth having in writing:

**The stream stops being append-only.** A branch is an interior deletion, and it can land in a day file from months ago — so **no day file is ever final**. Portal's append-union merge handles this gracefully by design (its prefix test fails and reconciliation falls to ordinary textual merge), and under D12 that path is rare anyway. The thing to remember is negative: any later optimization assuming historical immutability is now invalid. Cheap to know, expensive to discover.

**"Update any bookmarks" turns out to be free.** D11 already made anchors inline text that travels with the range, and section entries reference them by name and resolve by lookup — so the bookmark finds its new home with no work, provided nothing caches the resolved path. What *can* break is an ordinary markdown link pointing into the branched range, and that needs to break visibly rather than silently.

Portal's hardest sub-problem here also evaporates: images travelling with the range, cross-repository copy-verify-delete, the whole apparatus. One directory instead of per-project bundles deletes it. That's now the second requirement this structure has dissolved rather than solved.

**A branched file leaves the dated stream, so it loses its date.** Dates come from the day-file structure; a branched file isn't a day file. It needs an origin date in frontmatter at branch time or it becomes an undated object in a system organized by date. That's a format decision, so it's in v1 regardless.

And one thing worth naming: with independent findability deferred, **the link left behind is v1's entire findability mechanism** for branched content. Not a courtesy note — the only path back.

## The spike, in `goal/discovery/spike-01-experiment.md`

Written as a contract, before building, so "it sort of works" isn't an available outcome.

The main idea is that the original one-big-spike plan **decomposes**, and decomposing front-loads the decisive test at nearly zero cost:

- **Spike A — the editing surface.** A plain browser page. No platform decision, no shell, no build system. An evening. And here's the thing I'd flag as the actual content of Q1: **the risk isn't rendering, it's vim operating over widgets.** Rendering an equation inline is well-trodden. What's untested is what `dd` does to a line containing a rendered equation, whether cursor motion through a widget behaves, whether visual-select spans one correctly, whether undo puts it back. That's where this either works or quietly doesn't, and it's easy to build a demo that looks great and never tests it.
- **Spike A′ — the same page on Android.** Half an hour. This retires D4's known weakness — that the editor choice might not port, and you wouldn't find out until v2 — for almost nothing. Best trade on the list.
- **Spike B — the OS boundary.** Print a range and paste an image, in a native Swift shell and in Electron. Tauri needs no third implementation; you've already measured it.
- **Spike C — the windowed document.** Thirty synthetic day files edited as one surface, per-region write-back, position restore. A weekend, and only worth doing if A passes.

Success and failure criteria are written for each, including the honest one for A: p99 keystroke-to-paint under 30ms with no queueing under burst, **but the subjective test is the real criterion** — the number is there to stop you talking yourself into something that feels wrong.

One deliberate exclusion, recorded rather than left silent: **candidate 1, the fully native editor, is not spiked.** Building vim and markdown rendering from scratch in AppKit is expensive and on your weakest ground, so it's only worth its price if A fails — at which point it reopens immediately.

Take a look at the criteria before building anything; that's the point of writing them down first. If they're right, Spike A is an evening's work and it either unblocks everything or changes the project.

One note on updating bookmarks: While we refer to anchors by name, resolution is always going to require both anchor name and filename, and so *something* is going to have to be updated. However, our set of filesets is finite and is quick to scan over, so updating those isn’t a crazy move.

Looking at the discovery spikes, is the idea that all of these would be throwaway tests that just validate components? My since is that A, A’, and B naturally fit that bill, but C is really “start building the real system.”

Now cutting Spike C from the discovery work:
Both corrections taken. `D11` and `D13` amended, Spike C removed from the discovery plan, and the discipline note added to `notes.md`.

## On bookmarks — you're right, and the win is narrower than I said

I was assuming anchor names are globally unique, and they can't be: over twenty years you'll reuse *talk notes* and *the argument* a dozen times each, and enforcing uniqueness puts friction on a gesture whose whole point is that it's cheap. So the address is **(file, anchor name)**, and moving a range between files does require maintenance.

What D11 actually buys is still the thing that matters, just stated correctly: **anchors survive text moving *within* a file for free.** That's the case triggered by every act of typing above a bookmark — constant, invisible, and exactly what a byte offset would break on. The residual fragility is confined to one rare, explicit, user-initiated operation. That's a good place for it to be.

Your fix is right for sections, and it suggests a general rule. There are two classes of referrer and they want opposite policies:

- **Sections are few, finite, and must resolve instantly** — so update them on write. A branch scans the filesets and rewrites. Bounded and deterministic, as you say.
- **Ordinary markdown links into a range are potentially anywhere in the corpus** — so updating them on write means a branch operation rewrites arbitrary files, which collides badly with "no day file is ever final." Better to resolve those **on read**: follow the link by scanning for the anchor, and if it's moved or ambiguous, surface a picker over candidates. That's Portal's D52 finding reused — viewing and choosing are independent, so a picker needs no default — and it turns a hard break into a soft ambiguity.

So: **maintenance policy chosen by cardinality**, not by uniform rule. Recorded that way.

Two small things that fall out and belong in the v1 format work: anchor names need only be unique *within a file*, and the branch operation should order itself **create, then update references, then delete from source** — same discipline as Portal's cross-repository move, where the worst case is duplicated content (visible, fixable) rather than dangling references.

## On Spike C — you caught a process error

C was construction wearing a spike's clothes. The test I should have applied and didn't: *is this empirically uncertain, or is it merely unbuilt?* Stitching a window of files into one document, writing back touched regions, restoring position — all of that is reachable by reasoning. The one genuinely unknown quantity in it is whether the editor stays fast at that document size, and Spike A already measures that. So C had no hypothesis it could fail.

Worse, it's the specific pitfall the process names: a prototype carried into production is debt from day one, and C is exactly the kind of thing you'd be tempted to keep.

It's now v1's first construction task, in `solution/components.md`, with its acceptance criteria written down since those *were* worth fixing: no visible seam at a boundary, saving touches only the files actually edited, an edit spanning a boundary written correctly to both sides, position correct on reload and still correct after content is appended to an earlier file.

One sequencing note that came out of removing it: it should follow Spike A rather than run beside it, because a poor latency result changes the window size and therefore the design.

---

That leaves the spike as **A** (an evening, in a browser), **A′** (half an hour, on the phone), **B** (an evening or two, two shells). All three are genuinely disposable and all three can fail.

The next protocol step after findings come back is either decision-guidance — if B produces a fork you have to price — or architecture design for v1, if it doesn't. But nothing more is worth writing until Spike A tells us whether vim survives contact with inline widgets.

One other thing falls out from what you’re describing: At the core of our software architecture has to be a class representing a file. Its API exposes concepts like the .md text of the file, the list of sections/anchors/tags within it, and so on, and its storage implementation handles things like segmenting it into multiple .md files. 

Another thing that seems to be core is the “set of filesets” in the directory, because we’ll need to iterate over them when updating indices. This suggests that maybe we have one class representing that collective set, which has APIs for getting individual filesets etc., and also for updating a link globally across those. It also has a storage implementation, which writes the individual fileset files.

A general pattern (and this is a broad one in engineering) is that of “WXZ separation.” In the X layer of the API, objects should represent the natural, logical objects of the API — files, indices, and so on. Their exposed API represents the conceptual operations on those objects, and is used by the Z layer, i.e. the individual features of the system and UI. Their implementation manages how this concept is translated into the language of the underlying W layer of infrastructure, e.g. files on disks. We should make sure to make this layered separation clear and explicit in the code. 

Let’s make sure we capture that, and then I’ll start on spike 1.

## D14: Explicit W / X / Z layering, with Document and FilesetCollection as the core objects

**Date:** 2026-08-12
**Status:** decided
**Detail:** `solution/architecture.md`

**Decision.** The code is explicitly layered. **W** is infrastructure — files, directory watching, atomic replacement, OS services, and later the network hub. **X** is the logical objects of the domain, exposing conceptual operations and translating them into W's language. **Z** is the features and UI, consuming X. The core X objects are **Document** (one logical markdown document, whose storage implementation handles day-file segmentation) and **FilesetCollection** (the set of filesets, which can update a reference globally across them), alongside Corpus, Fileset, Query and Range.

**Why it is not merely a style preference here.** The most alarming finding Portal produced was a layering violation: a widget that opened its file during view construction re-read constantly and lost edit state on reparenting — R1.2, *no state is ever at risk*, failing at the framework level rather than in application logic. Separating model construction from view construction is the same rule as Z never reaching into W.

**Two things this makes true that were previously only descriptions.** "The notebook is one document" (D8) becomes real in code, since Document is one interface with two storage implementations — segmented for the stream, single-file for branched documents and pinned lists. And "update references on branch" (D11, D13) has an owner, since FilesetCollection is the only object that can see all filesets at once.

**The six rules that keep it honest** are in `solution/architecture.md`. The one that would otherwise be discovered painfully: **the layering is strict for operations and persistence, and deliberately loose for reading live state.** R1.1 is a hard latency requirement, and an editing surface routing every keystroke through Z→X→W cannot meet it — the live buffer is held in memory and rendered from directly, while X persists asynchronously. A naively strict version of this architecture would violate the project's primary requirement.
EOF

content:
This is the right spine, and it has one non-obvious consequence I want to flag. Capturing it first.
Captured in `solution/architecture.md` (with the structure diagram and trust boundaries), `system-design.json`, and **D14**.

Recording it surfaced five things worth having written down, one of which I think would have bitten:

**The layering has to be loose in exactly one place.** R1.1 is a hard latency requirement, and an editing surface that routes every keystroke Z→X→W will not make it. So: **strict for operations and persistence, deliberately loose for reading live state.** The live buffer sits in memory and the editor renders straight from it; X persists asynchronously; W writes atomically. A naively pure version of this architecture violates the project's primary requirement, which is the kind of thing that gets discovered three months in when the fix is expensive.

**Document is one interface with two storage implementations** — segmented for the stream, single-file for branched documents and pinned lists. That's what makes "the notebook is one document" (D8) true in code rather than only in prose. But it's also the arrangement in which D8's split rule quietly drifts toward being size-based and runtime-chosen, so: **the rule belongs to the format spec; storage merely obeys it.**

**`branch(range)` must be a single X operation.** Create-new, update-references, delete-from-source, in that order, is the only safety mechanism available without a cross-object transaction. If Z assembles it from three primitives, the ordering guarantee is gone and the failure mode is dangling references.

**The Corpus is allowed to reach W directly for bulk scans.** Search built as "for each Document, fetch text, scan" re-reads the world. The concept lives at X, the mechanism is a directory-level scan at W — that's the layering working rather than being violated, but it has to be stated or it gets built as N calls through Document.

**X owns the quiesce protocol** — flush, release, mutate, reload — because it's the only layer that knows about both in-flight edits and files. That's dormant in v1 and load-bearing in v2, when the sync client starts mutating files under a live editor.

I also drafted a preliminary threat list from decisions already taken (T1 silent loss on reconcile, T2 interrupted write, T7 cache eviction discarding unpushed text, T5 silent watcher death, plus the two open ones: hub compromise given that the notes discuss people who never consented to it, and Android TLS trust inherited unclosed from Portal). It's marked preliminary — proper failure analysis is its own process and hasn't run.

---

One thing for the spike: **none of this architecture should appear in Spike A.** It's a browser page with CodeMirror, a vim keymap, three widget types, and a latency counter — and it's disposable. If you find yourself introducing a Document class, that's the drift the process warns about.

Go build it. When findings come back, the criteria to judge against are in `goal/discovery/spike-01-experiment.md` as written — and the sharp part is vim over widgets, not rendering.

Yes but I would make one change to this: Instead of “the corpus is allowed to reach W directly for bulk scans,” search is implemented as its own X-level API. The dumbest first implementation of this will be reading files using the X layer file API — remember that “which file on disk holds this part of this lab notebook” isn’t really clear at the W layer — and a later implementation will maintain its own index, which the X-layer File implementation will be updating.

input.old_string: **4. The Corpus may reach W directly for bulk operations.** Search implemented as "for each Document, fetch text, scan" re-reads the world. The *concept* lives at X; the *mechanism* is a bulk scan of the directory at W. That is the layering working, not being violated — but it has to be said, or it gets built as N calls through Document.
input.new_string:
**4. Search is an X-level component with a swappable implementation, never a W-level scan.** The tempting optimization is to grep the directory directly. It is wrong for four reasons, any one of which is sufficient. **W does not know which file on disk holds a given part of the notebook** — that mapping belongs to Document's storage implementation, so a W-level result cannot be expressed as a position in the logical document. **W does not know the format**, so a raw scan matches frontmatter keys, tag markup and anchor syntax as though they were prose — the "don't contort a file format to suit a generic algorithm" rule, inverted. **A W-level hit is a file and a byte offset**, which is precisely the address D11 forbids. And **unsaved edits live in X's in-memory buffer**, so a disk scan cannot find the paragraph just typed.

The performance worry that motivated the shortcut does not materialize before its own fix does: v1's corpus scans in milliseconds, and by the time scanning is slow enough to notice, the index has arrived on its own merits.

**Two implementations behind one interface.** v1 reads through the Document API and scans. Later, Search maintains an index, kept current by Document — and the direction of that coupling matters: **Document emits change events and Search subscribes**, rather than Document calling Search. Document stays ignorant of its consumers, so a second index later (backlinks, tags) needs no change to it.

**An incrementally-maintained index needs a repair path or it becomes T6.** Events can be missed, an update can be interrupted, and a file can be hand-edited while the app is closed. The watcher covers hand-edits made while it is running; a **cheap consistency check at startup, with full rebuild on disagreement**, covers the rest. D7 already makes the index disposable, which is what makes rebuilding the correct response rather than a repair.

You're right, and my rule 4 was worse than premature — it relocated knowledge into a layer that can't hold it.
Corrected in `architecture.md`, `system-design.json`, and D14. Your version is right and my rule was wrong on more counts than the one you named:

- **W doesn't know which file holds what** — the day-file mapping belongs to Document's storage implementation, so a W-level result can't even be expressed as a position in the logical document.
- **W doesn't know the format**, so a raw scan happily matches frontmatter keys, tag markup and anchor syntax as though they were prose. That's exactly the "don't contort a file format to suit a generic algorithm" rule, inverted — I'd written the violation into an architecture document that cites the rule elsewhere.
- **A W-level hit is a file and a byte offset**, which is the address D11 forbids. Search would have been the one component manufacturing the thing everything else avoids.
- **Unsaved edits live in X's buffer**, so a disk scan can't find the paragraph you just typed. That one's a correctness bug, not a purity complaint.

And the optimization bought nothing anyway: v1's corpus scans in milliseconds, and by the time scanning is slow enough to notice, the index has arrived on its own merits. The problem never arrives before its own fix. I've put that in `notes.md` as a check to run before granting any layering exception for performance.

Two things I'd add to your version, both small:

**Direction of the coupling.** Document should *emit change events* and Search subscribe, rather than Document calling Search. Document then stays ignorant of its consumers, so a second index later — backlinks, tags — needs no change to it.

**An incremental index needs a repair path, or it becomes T6.** Events get missed, updates get interrupted, and files get hand-edited while the app is closed. The watcher covers hand-edits made while it's running; a cheap consistency check at startup with a full rebuild on disagreement covers the rest. D7 already makes the index disposable, which is what makes "rebuild" the right response rather than "repair."

Search also absorbed Query in the object table — one X component executing tag, date and text queries, which is what D9 said unifies anyway. Six X objects: Document, Corpus, Fileset, FilesetCollection, Search, Range.

Go build Spike A. The criteria are in `goal/discovery/spike-01-experiment.md`; the thing most likely to be quietly wrong is vim over widgets, not rendering.

# The Document API

The first artifact of v1's construction, ahead of the format spec. Written against D8, D11, D13, D14 and D16.

## Why this comes before the format

Syntax is convertible after the fact; **coverage is not.** A tag delimiter can be rewritten by a script, frontmatter keys renamed, filenames restructured — none of that strands anything. What cannot be recovered is a *fact the format never had a place for*: an origin date never written, a tag never recorded, a distinction the syntax could not express. That is the backfill rule (`notes.md`) applied precisely — and the set of facts that must be recordable is exactly the set the API exposes. So the API defines the format's obligations, and designing it first makes coverage fall out rather than be guessed at.

**One deadline worth naming.** Conversion is cheap while there is one device, one build, and downtime is free. It stops being cheap when v2 ships: two devices, one possibly mid-sync, and an older build on the phone reading files a newer build wrote. **The format must be settled before sync, not before v1.** That is real slack, but it is finite.

## A note on the name

The object is **Document**, not File. Calling it File invites precisely the confusion the abstraction exists to prevent — the stream is not a file, it is a logical document that happens to be stored across many. Files appear nowhere in this API.

## Two kinds of address, and they must not be confusable

This is the load-bearing distinction in the whole API.

```
Position  { doc: DocumentId, generation: int, offset: int }   // live, transient
Range     { from: Position, to: Position }                    // live, transient
Anchor    { name: string }                                    // durable, identity-based
```

**Positions are live state and carry a generation.** They are valid only against the document version they were taken from. Any change not made through the handle that holds them — a reload after external mutation, a sync pull, a hand-edit picked up by the watcher — advances the generation.

**A stale Position must fail loudly, never resolve approximately.** This is the API's single most important safety property. T1 (silent loss) is the top threat in `architecture.md`, and its most likely mechanism is an operation computed against text that has since moved: a queued tag, a branch, a print. Rejecting a stale Position converts that whole class into a visible error.

**Anchors are the durable form**, per D11. Nothing persisted ever holds a Position.

```
resolve(anchor) -> Position | NotFound        // may fail; failure is visible, never silent
anchorAt(position, name) -> Anchor            // creates one
```

## Windowing, expressed in domain terms

D8 requires the app to see one document; reality requires that tens of megabytes are not resident. The reconciliation is that **the window is expressed in dates, never in files.**

```
open(id) -> Document
Document.window(around: Date, extent: Duration) -> DocumentWindow
DocumentWindow.text -> string                 // what the editor binds to
DocumentWindow.extend(direction) -> void      // scrolling outward
```

For a branched document or a pinned list the window is the whole document, so one interface covers both and the stream is simply the case where the window is smaller than the whole. Files never appear. The segmentation rule stays a *format* obligation that storage obeys (D8), not a storage discretion.

## The facts the API exposes — this is the format's required coverage

Everything here must have a representation, or it is lost forever rather than merely awkward.

| Fact | Shape | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Text** | `window.text` | Markdown, one syntax family (D6) |
| **Date of a position** | `dateAt(position) -> Date` | Total, ordered, immutable (D9). Constant across a branched document — which is where the origin date is needed (D13) |
| **Anchors** | `anchors() -> [Anchor]`, `resolve` | Bookmarks. Inline, travelling with the text |
| **Tags on ranges** | `tags() -> [(Subject, Range)]` | Partial, mutable, **freely overlapping** (D9, R12). See below — this is the hard one |
| **Structure** | `headings() -> [(level, text, Position)]` | Nav, print, and naming a branched file |
| **Document metadata** | `meta` | Kind, origin date and origin link for branched documents |
| **Links** | `links() -> [Link]` | Including links to anchors, which resolve on read and may surface a picker (D11) |
| **Referenced images** | `images() -> [Path]` | Pasted files, so print and export can find them |
| **Dirty state** | `isDirty`, `lastSaved` | R1.2 |

## Operations

```
edit(range, text)                       // the primitive; everything else composes from it
append(text)                            // the common case, and the merge-safe one
tag(range, subject) / untag(range, subject)
setAnchor(position, name) / removeAnchor(anchor)
branch(range, name) -> DocumentId       // ONE operation (D13), never composed by Z
```

**`branch` is atomic at this layer by construction**, ordered create → update references → delete from source. Exposing its steps separately would put the ordering guarantee in Z's hands, where it will eventually be got wrong; the worst case then is dangling references rather than duplicated content.

**Tagging is a text edit**, since a persisted tag is inline markup (D11). That is a feature: it undoes, syncs and merges as ordinary text with no special machinery.

## The hard part: overlapping tags

R12 requires that subjects overlap freely — it is the property that made subjects-as-tags beat notebooks-as-containers. **Inline delimiters cannot express overlap**, because markup nests and overlapping ranges do not. Tag A over lines 3–8 and tag B over 6–12 have no well-nested form.

The API's obligation is therefore stated rather than dodged: **a tag has identity, applies to a range, and may interleave with any other tag.** How the format achieves that is the format spec's problem, but only some answers work, and the shape of the answer matters enough to flag now.

**The promising direction — and it deletes a concept.** Paired point markers interleave freely where nested delimiters cannot: A-start, B-start, A-end, B-end is perfectly well-formed as four independent points. And a point marker by identity is exactly what an anchor already is. So **anchors are the primitive: a bookmark is one anchor, a tagged range is a named pair.** One mechanism instead of two, overlap for free, and it fits D11 without strain.

Two costs to weigh when the format is written, not now:

- **Unbalanced pairs after hand-editing** need a defined degradation. Hand-editing is a feature, so this will happen.
- **The markers are visible in raw mode**, which is a first-class editing surface. This is less alarming than it sounds — D16's widget layer already unrenders constructs under the cursor and renders them away from it, which is exactly the affordance needed.

## Lifecycle, events, and external mutation

```
Document.on('changed', (ranges) => ...)   // Document stays ignorant of its consumers (D14)
flush() / release() / reload()            // the quiesce protocol, owned by X (D14 rule 3)
```

**External mutation while edits are unsaved is the one case that must not be automated.** The watcher reports a file changed underneath; if the document is clean, reload. If it is dirty, the two versions diverge and **Document surfaces rather than choosing** — the same picker discipline as D12, for the same reason: no default here is a recommendation the system has any basis for. Rare under D12, but "rare" is why it has to be handled deliberately rather than by whatever the code happens to do.

## Deliberately not in v1

TODO fields; fileset entry types beyond what the nav needs; rendered-editing per node type (staged separately per Q1); the index and its change-feed consumer (D7 — Search scans in v1); anything about sync beyond the generation counter that makes reloads safe.

## What this leaves for the format spec

Day-file naming and the split rule; frontmatter keys, including the branched-file origin date; anchor syntax; the tag representation, constrained by the overlap requirement above; and how each of these degrades when a human has been editing by hand.

```

# The Document API

v1's first artifact, ahead of the format spec. Written against D8, D11, D13, D14, D16, D18, D19, D20.

## Why this comes before the format

Syntax is convertible after the fact; **coverage is not.** Delimiters can be rewritten, keys renamed, files restructured — none of that strands anything. What cannot be recovered is a fact the format never had a place for. The set of facts that must be recordable is exactly the set this API exposes.

**The deadline:** conversion is cheap with one device, one build, and free downtime. It stops being cheap at v2 — two devices, one possibly mid-sync, an older build reading files a newer one wrote. **The format must be settled before sync, not before v1.**

The object is **Document**, not File. Files appear nowhere in this API.

---

## The model

A Document is a **potentially unbounded markdown stream** containing **Spans**. A Span has a kind (date, heading, anchor, tag, …), a name (the date, the subject, the anchor's label), and an id.

**Spans are inferred from the text, never stored alongside it.** Date spans come from file frontmatter; headings from markdown headings; anchors from anchor markers; tags from a delimited tagging protocol the format defines. Nothing maintains a parallel span store.

This is the simplification that carries the most weight elsewhere:

- **The document is a pure function of its text.** No side state to keep consistent, nothing to go stale.
- **Hand-editing works structurally rather than by effort.** Edit the markdown, the spans change. The discipline that every format must survive a human editing it is satisfied by construction.
- **Merge is text merge.** There is no span merge, ever.
- **There is exactly one mutation.** Creating a tag is inserting marker text; creating an anchor is inserting marker text; creating a heading is typing `##`. An earlier draft had a rule that the API must be "read-uniform and write-differentiated" — inference **deletes that rule**. The semantic tier is a set of text generators over one write primitive, not a second write path.

Spans may also be constructed with no textual basis at all: a search result, an explicit range, the user's current selection. These are ordinary Spans and every operation accepts them.

## Addressing

```
Span   { begin, end }        // half-open, [begin, end)
```

**A Span is never persisted — and neither is a span id.** For authored spans (anchors, tags) the durable handle is the *name*, which lives in the text. For inferred spans (headings, dates) the id is a handle valid within one generation, with exactly the same status as an offset: useful now, meaningless later. Anything durable references a name (D11).

Spans carry a **generation**. Any change not made through the holding handle — a reload after external mutation, a sync pull, a hand-edit caught by the watcher — advances it, and **a stale Span must fail loudly rather than resolve approximately.** T1 (silent loss) is the top threat, and its likeliest mechanism is an operation computed against text that has since moved.

**Open: the offset unit** (D20). Code points are the principled choice; **both target platforms are natively UTF-16** — JavaScript and Kotlin alike — so code points cost a conversion at every boundary with CodeMirror, on the path R1.1 governs. Astral characters will occur here: mathematical alphanumerics live above the BMP. Whichever is chosen, the invariant is that a Span never splits a surrogate pair. Note also that `size` is O(1) in bytes or UTF-16 units and O(n) in code points.

## Reading

The operations appropriate to an unbounded buffer:

```
size() -> int
fetch(span) -> { span, text }     // markdown-aware; may return more than asked
snap(span) -> span                // the same widening, without fetching text
```

**Fetch is markdown-aware.** If either end lands inside a heading, a table or an equation, the returned span widens to contain the whole construct — so it returns the span it actually served, not only the bytes.

**Returning the actual span is load-bearing, not a courtesy.** It is what makes read-modify-write correct: `const {span, text} = fetch(s)` followed by `replace(span, edited)` operates on exactly what was read. A fetch that returned only bytes would make that natural idiom silently wrong.

`snap` exists because the editor's widget layer needs construct boundaries constantly and does not need the text again.

## Writing

```
replace([{ span, payload }, ...]) -> void
```

**The primitive is a batch, and the single edit is the special case.** An empty span is an insert; an empty payload is a delete.

**It must be a batch for three reasons, and the first is a correctness one.** Tagging a range is *two* insertions. As two calls, the document passes through a state with an unbalanced marker that a change-event consumer will observe, and the second call's offsets must be adjusted by the first — arithmetic in the caller, which is where it will eventually be got wrong. As one transaction, offsets are all relative to the pre-state, there is no transient invalid document, and undo granularity matches what the user thinks they did.

## Undo has to be single-sourced

The one architectural hazard in this design. CodeMirror keeps its own history; Document is the model. Two histories over the same text will diverge — type a sentence, apply a tag through the API, undo, and the result depends on which stack answers.

**The rule: for a document open in an editor, the editor's transaction system is the write path and `replace` is what it calls. For a document not open — updating fileset references during a branch, for instance — Document writes directly.** One history per document at a time, and the boundary is whether an editor holds it.

## Durability

The contract deserves stating precisely, because a naive reading of it collides head-on with R1.1.

**`replace` is durable on return — but the keystroke path does not call `replace` per keystroke.** The editor holds the live buffer (D14 rule 6) and renders from it; typing is not a sequence of API calls. `replace` is the path for *operations* — tag, branch, programmatic edit — which are rare enough that synchronous durability costs nothing.

**What then guarantees typed text?** This is where the realistic failure mode matters, and it is not power loss. **The live buffer lives in the renderer process, and the renderer is the component most likely to die.** Durability must therefore cross to the main process quickly and cheaply.

Rewriting a day file per keystroke is not cheap. An **append is** — and the notebook is append-shaped anyway, which is the same property that makes its merge rule work. So the two candidate contracts are:

- **Durable-on-append.** Keystrokes append to a journal in the main process; the day file is rewritten on quiescence; a crash replays the journal. Satisfies "losing anything, ever" literally.
- **Durable-on-quiescence.** Debounced autosave, no journal. Worst case loses the last few hundred milliseconds of typing — which satisfies R1.2 psychologically and violates it literally.

**These are API-compatible**, so the choice can be deferred *if* the contract is stated now as: durable when `flush()` resolves, and durable within N ms otherwise. Fixing N later is not a breaking change; discovering there was never a contract is.

## Lifecycle and external mutation

```
Document.on('changed', (spans) => ...)   // Document stays ignorant of its consumers (D14)
flush() / release() / reload()           // the quiesce protocol, owned by X
branch(span, name) -> DocumentId         // one operation, never composed by Z (D13)
```

**External mutation while edits are unsaved must not be automated.** Clean document, reload. Dirty document, the versions have diverged and Document **surfaces rather than choosing** — the picker discipline of D12, for the same reason: a default would be a recommendation the system has no basis for.

## Two leaks to close in the semantic tier

**Adjacent same-date spans must coalesce.** Date spans are inferred from per-file frontmatter, so a within-day split — the 50 MB day — produces two files bearing the same date and therefore two adjacent date spans. If the semantic tier does not merge them, storage segmentation becomes visible above the API, which is the one thing D8 and D19 exist to prevent.

**Document-level metadata is not a span.** Kind, origin date and origin link for branched documents (D13) are properties of the whole document. Forcing them into the span model is the generalization going one step too far.

## What this leaves for the format spec

Frontmatter keys, including the per-file date and the branched-file origin (D13); anchor marker syntax; the tag protocol, constrained by overlap — paired point markers interleave where nested delimiters cannot, which makes a bookmark an unpaired anchor and a tag a named pair; the split rule and its coordination requirement (D19); and how each degrades when a human has been editing by hand.

**One constraint to notice while writing it.** Carrying the date in per-file frontmatter has the *same* limitation as carrying it in the filename: one file, one date, so days can be split but never coalesced. That is very likely fine — twenty years is a few thousand files, and nothing wants coalescing — but it should be a decision rather than a side effect. The fully general alternative is a date marker within the text, at the cost of noise in the raw view.

**The deadline:** conversion is cheap with one device, one build, and free downtime. It stops being cheap at v2. **The format must be settled before sync, not before v1.**

The object is **Document**, not File. Files appear nowhere in this API.

---

## The model

A Document is a **potentially unbounded markdown stream** containing **Spans**. A Span has a kind (date, heading, anchor, tag) and a name — the date, the subject, the anchor's label. It has **no id**: with inference there is nothing for one to identify, and a durable handle is always the name in the text.

**Spans are inferred from the text, never stored beside it.** Dates come from frontmatter, headings from markdown headings, anchors from anchor markers, tags from a delimited protocol the format defines.

- **The document is a pure function of its text.** No side state, nothing to go stale.
- **Hand-editing works structurally.** Edit the markdown, the spans change.
- **Merge is text merge.** There is no span merge.
- **There is one mutation.** Creating a tag is inserting marker text; the semantic tier is a set of text generators over a single primitive.

Spans may also have no textual basis: a search result, an explicit range, the current selection. These are ordinary Spans and every operation accepts them.

## Three coordinate systems, and only one of them is a design choice

This is where the bugs live, so all three are named.

| | Coordinates | Who uses them |
|---|---|---|
| **Document** | `(date, offset)` | The API, search results, nav targets |
| **Window** | offset into the loaded buffer | The editor, internally |
| **Storage** | `(file, offset)` | Below Document, never exposed |

**Document coordinates are `(date, offset)`, not an absolute offset into the infinite stream.** The absolute form is conceptually tidier and worse in two concrete ways. It requires a global index of every file's length to compute any position — and length in characters, not bytes, so `stat` will not do it. And more seriously, **it makes every position in the corpus stale after any edit anywhere**: inserting a sentence into a 2020 entry shifts every 2026 offset. With `(date, offset)`, an edit invalidates only positions within that date, which matters because search results, nav targets and section entries all hold positions.

`(date, offset)` also survives the 50 MB-day case cleanly: a within-day split changes the date→files mapping and nothing above it. The ordering is lexicographic — compare dates, then offsets — and a Span may span dates.

**A Span carries a generation, and a stale Span must fail loudly** rather than resolve approximately. T1 (silent loss) is the top threat, and its likeliest mechanism is an operation computed against text that has since moved. Nothing durable holds a Span (D11).

**Open: the offset unit** (D20). Code points are principled; both target platforms are natively UTF-16, and CodeMirror is UTF-16 throughout, so code points cost a conversion on the path R1.1 governs. Astral characters will occur — mathematical alphanumerics live above the BMP. The invariant either way: a Span never splits a surrogate pair.

## The CodeMirror alignment

CodeMirror 6's core is `@codemirror/state`, which has **no DOM dependency** — it is a rope, a transaction system and a state container that happen to be maintained alongside an editor. Its model is already the one we designed:

- `EditorState` is immutable; `state.update(spec)` yields a `Transaction` whose `.state` is the successor.
- A change spec is `{from, to, insert}` or **an array of them, relative to the pre-state, sorted and non-overlapping** — which is exactly `replace([{span, payload}])`.
- A `ChangeSet` can be inverted, composed, mapped through other changes, and **serialised** (`toJSON`/`fromJSON`).
- `history()` (from `@codemirror/commands`) is a StateField that observes transactions and groups them by a configurable delay and by `userEvent` annotation. Transactions can opt out with the `addToHistory` annotation, or force an event boundary with `isolateHistory`.

**So Document's buffer *is* an `EditorState`.** The view attaches when the document is open and detaches when it is not; the state exists either way. This is the unification the parallelism was worth looking for, and it dissolves the problem rather than managing it.

## What that buys

**The undo conflict disappears rather than being arbitrated.** There are not two histories to reconcile — there is one, living in a StateField, and every mutation is a transaction. The earlier rule about "open documents write through the editor, closed documents write directly" is **deleted**: there is no distinction, because a headless `EditorState` takes the same transactions as one with a view.

Two consequences worth taking deliberately:

- **Programmatic operations should carry `isolateHistory`**, so applying a tag is its own undo step rather than merging into the sentence you were typing. Undo granularity should match intent, and here it is a one-line annotation.
- **Externally-originated changes carry `addToHistory: false`** — a sync pull, a watcher reload — and history maps its stored events through them, so undo still works afterwards. This is exactly what the collaborative-editing package does, and it is the mechanism v2's sync layer will want.

**The durability contract simplifies to something small.** If every mutation is a transaction, the journal is **a log of serialised ChangeSets**: append on transaction, replay on crash, compose and discard when the file is rewritten at quiescence. `ChangeSet.compose` also means the journal compacts for free. That makes the strict contract — nothing is ever lost, not even the last keystroke — cheap enough that there is little reason to take the weaker one.

The contract, stated so it cannot be forgotten: **durable when `flush()` resolves, and durable within N ms otherwise.** The realistic loss event is not power failure but a **renderer crash**, since the live buffer lives in the renderer; the journal has to cross to the main process, which is why it must be an append and not a file rewrite.

**And a small R1.2 win that is nearly free.** `EditorState` can serialise its history field, so **the undo stack can survive an app restart.** "No state is ever at risk" arguably includes it, most applications drop it, and this one would be noticed.

**The bet this makes, named rather than assumed.** Building Document on `@codemirror/state` couples the model layer to a JavaScript library. That is defensible because the package is DOM-free, and because Spike A′ found the same page runs well on Android — so if the phone is also a web build, the same code serves. If Android is ever native Kotlin, the *contract* ports and the *implementation* does not. That is a real cost, and it is an argument for the phone being web-based too.

## Reading

```
extent() -> (firstDate, lastDate)
fetch(span) -> { span, text }     // markdown-aware; may return more than asked
snap(span) -> span                // the same widening, without fetching text
```

**Fetch is markdown-aware**: if either end lands inside a heading, table or equation, the returned span widens to contain the whole construct. **Returning the actual span is load-bearing, not a courtesy** — it makes `fetch` → edit → `replace(returnedSpan)` correct, where a bytes-only fetch would make that natural idiom silently wrong. `snap` exists because the widget layer needs construct boundaries constantly and does not need the text again.

## Writing

```
replace([{ span, payload }, ...]) -> void
```

A batch, with the single edit as the special case; empty span inserts, empty payload deletes. It **must** be a batch: tagging a range is two insertions, and as two calls the document passes through a state with an unbalanced marker that a change consumer will observe, while the second call's offsets must be adjusted by the first — arithmetic in the caller, which will eventually be got wrong.

## Lifecycle and external mutation

```
Document.on('changed', (spans) => ...)   // Document stays ignorant of its consumers (D14)
flush() / release() / reload()           // the quiesce protocol, owned by X
branch(span, name) -> DocumentId         // one operation, never composed by Z (D13)
```

**External mutation while edits are unsaved must not be automated.** Clean document, reload. Dirty document, the versions have diverged and Document **surfaces rather than choosing** — the picker discipline of D12.

## Two leaks the semantic tier must close

**Adjacent same-date spans must coalesce**, or a within-day split makes storage segmentation visible above the API — the thing D8 and D19 exist to prevent.

**Document-level metadata is not a span.** Kind, origin date and origin link for branched documents (D13) are properties of the whole document.

## What this leaves for the format spec

Frontmatter keys, including the per-file date and the branched-file origin; anchor marker syntax; the tag protocol, constrained by overlap — paired point markers interleave where nested delimiters cannot, making a bookmark an unpaired anchor and a tag a named pair; the split rule and its coordination requirement (D19); and how each degrades under hand-editing.

**One constraint to notice while writing it.** Carrying the date in per-file frontmatter has the same limitation as carrying it in the filename: one file, one date, so days can be split but never coalesced. Very likely fine — twenty years is a few thousand files and nothing wants coalescing — but a decision rather than a side effect.

Good question — the answer collapses three of our open problems at once. Let me lay out what CodeMirror actually provides, then what it buys.
## What CodeMirror actually gives you

The core is **`@codemirror/state`**, which has no DOM dependency — it's a rope, a transaction system, and a state container that happen to be maintained alongside an editor.

- **`EditorState` is immutable.** `state.update(spec)` returns a `Transaction` whose `.state` is the successor. A view dispatches transactions; a headless state accepts them identically.
- **A change spec is `{from, to, insert}`, or an array of them — relative to the pre-state, required to be sorted and non-overlapping.** That is `replace([{span, payload}])`, arrived at independently and matching exactly.
- **`ChangeSet`** can be inverted, composed, mapped through other changes, and serialised (`toJSON`/`fromJSON`).
- **`history()`** (in `@codemirror/commands`) is a StateField observing transactions, grouping by a configurable delay and by `userEvent` annotation. Transactions opt out with the `addToHistory` annotation, or force an event boundary with `isolateHistory`.
- Positions are UTF-16 code units throughout.

## So make Document's buffer *be* an EditorState

That's the parallelism you were reaching for, and it dissolves three problems rather than managing them. Recorded as **D21**.

**The undo conflict is deleted, not arbitrated.** There aren't two histories to reconcile — there's one StateField, and every mutation is a transaction. My rule from last round about open documents writing through the editor and closed ones writing directly is **withdrawn**: a headless `EditorState` takes the same transactions as one with a view, so the distinction never existed. That was me solving a problem that only appeared because I'd assumed the model and the editor had to be different things.

**Durability becomes small.** If every mutation is a transaction, the journal is a log of serialised ChangeSets: append on transaction, replay after a crash, compose and discard when the file is rewritten at quiescence. `ChangeSet.compose` compacts it for free. That makes the strict contract — nothing lost, not even the last keystroke — cheap enough that there's little reason to take the weaker one. The realistic loss event is still a renderer crash, which is exactly why the journal must be an append crossing to main rather than a file rewrite.

**Two annotations do real work.** `isolateHistory` on programmatic operations, so applying a tag is its own undo step instead of merging into the sentence you were mid-way through typing. And `addToHistory: false` on externally-originated changes, with history mapping its stored events through them — that's how the collaborative-editing package handles remote edits, and it's the mechanism v2's sync layer will want.

**One nearly-free R1.2 win:** `EditorState` can serialise its history field, so the undo stack can survive an app restart. Most applications drop it. You'd notice.

**The bet, named rather than assumed:** this couples the model layer to a JavaScript library. Defensible because the package is DOM-free, and because A′ found the same page runs well on Android — so a web-based phone shares the code. If Android ever goes native Kotlin, the contract ports and the implementation doesn't. Worth knowing you're leaning on the phone being web-based.

**Span ids: agreed, dropped.** With inference there's nothing for one to identify, and the durable handle is always the name in the text.

## Your NB, and one recommendation inside it

You're right that there are Document-level positions distinct from storage positions — and it's actually three coordinate systems, which is worth naming because that's where this kind of bug lives: **Document** (the API), **window** (the loaded buffer, what CodeMirror sees), **storage** (`file, offset`, never exposed).

On the Document form, I'd argue for **`(date, offset)` rather than an absolute offset into the infinite stream.** The absolute version is tidier to describe and worse in two concrete ways:

- It needs a global index of every file's *character* length to compute any position, and `stat` can't supply that — you'd have to read the corpus.
- More seriously, **it makes every position in the corpus stale after any edit anywhere.** Insert a sentence into a 2020 entry and every 2026 offset shifts. With `(date, offset)`, an edit invalidates only positions within that date — which matters because search results, nav targets and section entries all hold positions, and under the fail-loudly rule a stale position is a hard error rather than a quiet wrong answer.

It also handles your 50 MB day cleanly: a within-day split changes the date→files mapping and nothing above it. Ordering is lexicographic, and a Span may cross dates.

---

The remaining open item in the API is the offset unit — UTF-16 versus code points — which is now a smaller question than it was, since aligning with `EditorState` makes UTF-16 the zero-friction choice and code points a deliberate conversion at the boundary. After that, the format spec.

Excellent. The one thing I would do is ensure that the Document API is written without *direct* reference to or dependency on the CodeMirror API, just compatibility — in case we ever need to change CodeMirror out, I think these primitives will continue to be useful and fundamental. 

I like your point about the (date, offset) structure. We should be quite explicit about the different kinds of position and make these named types within the code — DocumentPosition, WindowPosition, StoragePosition. (StoragePosition should never be getting exposed in the ordinary API, but we’ll use it a bunch internally!)

Let’s do a full rewrite of the Document API on this basis, and make it an explicit TypeScript API declaration.

`solution/document-api.md` is a full rewrite around the TypeScript declaration, recorded as **D22**.

## What the isolation cost

Almost nothing, which is the good news — the primitives turn out to be about the problem rather than about the library. A dated stream, spans inferred from text, one batched mutation, positions that expire. I've stated the alignment as **five properties any editor must satisfy**, rather than as a dependency:

1. Edits are a sorted, non-overlapping batch relative to the pre-edit state.
2. Window positions are integer offsets in the editor's own unit, so window↔document conversion is arithmetic.
3. Changes are serialisable — this is what makes the durability journal a log of change records.
4. Changes can map a held position through them.
5. Edits carry an origin annotation controlling history grouping and membership.

If CodeMirror is ever swapped out, that list is what has to be re-satisfied, not the API.

## Three things the declaration forced into the open

**Async versus sync is now a type-level statement.** `fetch` is async because arbitrary spans may name unloaded content; `DocumentWindow.text` is synchronous because the editor's hot path must never await. That's D14 rule 6 — strict for operations, loose for live state — expressed in signatures instead of prose, which is where it will actually be obeyed.

**`EditOrigin` carries the entire undo policy.** `'user' | 'operation' | 'external'` — typing groups, an applied tag is its own step, a sync pull doesn't enter history but gets mapped through. Putting it in the API rather than in editor configuration is what keeps the policy from becoming an accident of setup.

**`dateAt` came out synchronous**, which surprised me — the date is already inside `DocumentPosition`, so a query that looked like it needed a lookup is a field access. Small, but a sign the coordinate choice was the right one.

## One thing I'd flag before you build

**Windowing is in the API and may well not be needed in v1.** Spike A measured flat cost at 1.05 MB; year one of the corpus is roughly that; 25 MB is twenty years away. So v1 can legitimately return a window covering the whole document, and the type exists so windowing arrives later without an API change.

But it carries an unanswered question with it: **should undo survive a window move?** If the window is the whole document, one history, no question. If windowing arrives, scrolling to 2019, editing, and scrolling back raises a real question about what ⌘Z should then do. I've deferred it explicitly rather than letting the first implementation decide it silently.

## Still open in the API

The offset unit — UTF-16 code units versus code points. Aligning with the editor makes UTF-16 the zero-friction choice and code points a deliberate conversion at the boundary; either is defensible, and the invariant is that no position splits a surrogate pair. That's the last thing in this document that isn't settled.

The format spec is next, and its brief is now tight: frontmatter keys including the per-file date and branched-file origin, anchor marker syntax, the tag protocol constrained by overlap, the split rule and its coordination requirement, and how each degrades under hand-editing.

I can promise you that I will push the windowing boundary far faster than you think. In Era 3, a typical month was producing maybe 40-50 thousand lines of text. 

And yes, undo needs to survive this; window moves are about which part of the rope is visible in the editor, and are completely orthogonal to the concept of editing. Spans are (correctly) defined in terms of DocumentPosition; undos should affect the history of the document. Essentially, DocumentPosition is the “true” position within the API and everything else needs to be derived from it.

One way to think of it is that a different storage architecture we could use is journal+digest: we have one file that’s just a sequence of DocumentChange records with timestamps in them, and zero or more snapshots at fixed timestamps that are “realized” versions of the file as a directory full of text files or whatever. Reading the state of the file at time t means reading the last digest prior to t and then applying all edits between that digest’s timestamp and t, and undo is simply scrolling backwards in this space. In a world like this, the meaning of an undo is clear, and the fact that it has nothing to do with a window likewise becomes obvious. 

Really, what a “read” operation becomes is “load the window at this given span, adjusting span boundaries if needed to provide a meaningful output,” which is then a UX affordance so that the UX can render that particular subset, and make it quick and easy to edit it. Reads also happen at a generation.

Does that help resolve how undos and windows should interact?

## D23: Undo is document-scoped; windows are a read affordance; journal+digest as model, not as storage

**Date:** 2026-08-12
**Status:** decided
**Detail:** `solution/document-api.md`
**Amends:** D21, D22

**The fact that forced this.** Era 3 produced 40–50 thousand lines a month — roughly **2–3.5 MB a month, 20–45 MB a year, 0.4–0.9 GB over twenty years**. Spike A's 1.05 MB corpus, which read as a generous test, is **about a fortnight of writing**.

**Decision.** `DocumentPosition` is the true position and everything else derives from it. **Undo is movement through the document's change history, in document space, entirely unrelated to what is on screen.** A window is a rendering affordance — load this region, widen its boundaries to something meaningful, make it fast to edit — holding no history and owning no state lost by closing it. Reads take a span *and a generation*.

**The clarifying model is journal plus digest**: a document is a sequence of change records with periodic realised snapshots; state at time *t* is the last snapshot before *t* plus everything since. Undo is scrolling backwards in that space, which makes its independence from windows obvious rather than argued.

**The model is adopted; the storage architecture is not.** Making the journal authoritative would demote the plain text files to a derived snapshot — which is exactly the fork Q2 closed in the opposite direction, arriving through a different door. **The journal is a write-ahead log over authoritative text**, folded in and discarded at quiescence. Retaining it past quiescence is a separate small choice that buys restart-surviving undo at the cost of a second representation.

**What this amends in D21.** D21 claimed the undo conflict was *deleted* because Document's buffer **was** an `EditorState`. At this corpus size that premise is false — the document does not fit in a buffer and never did. The conflict is therefore **relocated, not deleted**: there is exactly one history, it lives in Document in document space, the editor's own history is **disabled**, and undo/redo bind to `Document.undo`/`redo`. What survives of D21 is the transaction *shape* (D22's compatibility contract) and the serialisable-change model that makes the journal cheap. This is the "a rationale can expire when a later decision changes the substrate underneath it" discipline firing on a decision three hours old.

**Three consequences beyond the API.**
- **Windowing is required in v1**, not deferred. A month of writing is already 2.4× the largest thing the editor has been tested against.
- **The index arrives sooner than D7 assumed.** Scanning is instant at 10 MB and is not at 50 MB, which is year two. "Index is a v3 concern" was optimistic; plan it for v2.
- **Undo may land outside the current window**, so `undo()` returns the change and the UI moves there. An undo with no visible effect is worse than no undo.

## The arithmetic first

45k lines/month at 40–80 chars per line: **2–3.5 MB a month, 20–45 MB a year, 0.4–0.9 GB over twenty years.** Three of my estimates were wrong, one of them load-bearing:

- **Spike A's 1.05 MB corpus is about a fortnight of writing**, not "roughly year one." The flatness result stands; the language I wrapped around it overstated its range by ~25×.

## And it invalidates D21's central claim

D21 said the undo conflict was *deleted* because Document's buffer **was** an `EditorState`. That premise is false at this scale — the document doesn't fit in a buffer and never did. So the conflict isn't deleted, it's **relocated**: one history, living in Document, in document space; the editor's own history **disabled**; undo/redo bound to `Document.undo`/`redo`.

What survives of D21 is the part that was really about shape rather than residency — the transaction form in D22's compatibility contract, and the serialisable-change model that makes the journal cheap.

The model is exactly right and makes the answer obvious rather than argued: a document is a sequence of changes with periodic realised snapshots; undo is scrolling backwards in that space; a read is `(span, generation)`; a window is a rendering affordance that holds no history and owns nothing lost by closing it.

It's the CRDT trade wearing different clothes: conflict-free by construction, files become an export, R26 weakens. So: the journal is a **write-ahead log over authoritative text**, folded in and discarded at quiescence.

One small choice that falls out and is worth taking deliberately rather than by default: **retaining the journal past quiescence** buys undo that survives an app restart, at the cost of a second representation of the same data.

## Two API changes from this

**`fetch` and `window` collapse into one `read(span, at?)`** returning a Window — which is your framing exactly: load this region, widen the boundaries to something meaningful, hand back what was actually served. The `at` parameter for reading a historical generation is in the signature even though v1 may only support the current one, because diffing and the divergence picker will want it and it shouldn't cost an API change.

**`undo()` returns the `DocumentChange` rather than a boolean**, because undo can land outside the current window — and an undo with no visible effect is worse than no undo. The UI is expected to move to where the change happened.

---

Everything else here is settled, and the format spec's brief is unchanged — though the volume figure makes one of its notes easier: at 2–3.5 MB a month, days will want *splitting* long before they want merging, so the one-file-one-date constraint costs nothing.

Excellent, and this is good. Now as far as the offset, we have an interesting challenge in that the editors work in UTF16, but nobody wants to serialize UTF16 to disk or basically ever deal with it (Java’s choice to do this was idiosyncratic to say the least); everything in the world works in UTF8. 

We might actually want different types of offset in different types of position. Let’s make a list of some of the alternatives and discuss their pros and cons.

# Offset units — options and analysis

The last open item in the Document API (D20). Not yet decided.

## Where offsets actually appear

| Position | Consumer | Native unit of that consumer |
|---|---|---|
| `WindowPosition` | CodeMirror, in a loaded window | UTF-16 code units |
| `DocumentPosition.offset` | The API surface; spans; journal records | none — ours to choose |
| `StoragePosition.offset` | Locating a date's content within files | none — ours to choose |
| File I/O | Reading and writing files | UTF-8 bytes |

## Two facts that reframe the question

**1. Nothing durable holds an offset, by construction.** D11 already forbids it: bookmarks and tags are markers in the text, section entries reference names, links resolve by lookup. **The only serialised offsets anywhere are inside the journal**, which is a transient write-ahead log, discarded at quiescence, written and read by one build of one app. So "we would be serialising UTF-16" is a much smaller claim than it sounds — and it is also slightly mis-stated: the journal is UTF-8 JSON containing integers. We would never write UTF-16 *as an encoding* to disk. We would write a number whose semantics happen to be a count of UTF-16 code units.

**2. The document↔storage boundary is file-granular, not offset-granular.** Writes are whole-file atomic replacements; reads load whole files. At measured volume a day file is around 100 KB, so nothing ever needs to seek into an undecoded file. Byte offsets are therefore never *required* as an addressing unit — bytes appear only in operations that take no offsets at all.

Together these dissolve most of the case for bytes and most of the case against UTF-16.

**The remaining structural fact:** conversion is nearly free when it is a byproduct of a bulk transcode you are already doing — decoding a file on load, encoding it on save. It is expensive when it must be maintained incrementally against a buffer being edited at 130 WPM.

## The options

### 1. UTF-16 code units everywhere

Window, document and storage positions all in UTF-16; bytes confined to file I/O.

- **For:** zero conversion at the only boundary crossed on the hot path. Native to both target platforms — JavaScript and Kotlin alike. Simplest possible mental model: one unit, one invariant.
- **Against:** a JS/Java-era artifact promoted to a domain concept. If a future implementation is Rust or Swift, its native string type is UTF-8 and every position needs converting.
- **Cost of being wrong:** low, because no durable artifact records an offset.

### 2. Unicode code points everywhere

- **For:** principled and representation-independent.
- **Against:** **pays at both boundaries and gains none.** Code point↔UTF-16 needs surrogate counting; code point↔byte needs a scan. Nothing consumes code points natively. This is the worst of the three uniform options and is listed for completeness.

### 3. UTF-8 bytes everywhere

- **For:** matches disk, matches every external tool, matches Rust. Portable by default.
- **Against:** puts an incrementally-maintained conversion on the hot path. Every editor edit must translate UTF-16→bytes, which needs a prefix-sum structure over the buffer maintained under edits — a Fenwick tree or equivalent, O(log n) per operation, plus the code to keep it correct. Buys portability we have no consumer for, since rule 4 keeps search inside the Document API rather than handing it to ripgrep.

### 4. Split: UTF-16 in the window, bytes in document and storage

- **For:** the API's serialised form is portable; the storage boundary is free.
- **Against:** the *hot* boundary is the one that pays, which is exactly backwards. Same Fenwick-tree cost as option 3, for the same non-existent consumer.

### 5. Split: UTF-16 in window and document, bytes in storage only

- **For:** hot path free; conversion happens only during whole-file transcode, where it is a byproduct.
- **Against:** given fact 2 above, `StoragePosition` never actually needs byte semantics — files are decoded whole. So this option is **option 1 with an extra unit that earns nothing.**

### 6. Line-based document positions — `(date, line, column)`

The one genuinely different shape, and it deserves consideration rather than dismissal.

- **For:** lines are the granularity of merge — append-union and textual merge3 are both line-based — so positions would align with reconciliation instead of cutting across it. Line indices are stable under edits *within* other lines, which is better locality than character offsets. Columns are short, so any column-unit conversion is genuinely free. And it matches how this corpus is actually measured: "40–50 thousand lines a month."
- **Against:** a three-component position with lexicographic comparison, in an API where two-component positions were already the compromise. Line indices still shift when lines are added or removed, so it reduces rather than removes invalidation. And the locality argument is largely already won by the date partition — a single date holds roughly 1500 lines, so offsets within it are small numbers that shift rarely.
- **Verdict:** the merge alignment is a real argument and the only one that would justify the complexity. It is worth revisiting if the format spec finds that merge wants line addresses anyway.

### 7. Opaque `Offset` — orthogonal to all of the above

Make `Offset` a branded type with no public arithmetic: callers get spans from the API (`snap`, `read`, search results, selections) and combine them through Document helpers rather than doing sums.

- **For:** the unit becomes reversible. Given how much of this design has been revised under new information — twice today by a single fact — buying reversibility on a decision with no strong winner is worth something.
- **Against:** manual arithmetic is occasionally natural and would need helpers. Probably a small cost, since callers rarely construct offsets from nothing.

## Recommendation

**Option 1, with option 7 layered over it: UTF-16 code units, behind an opaque `Offset` type.**

The two reframing facts remove the objections that made bytes attractive — nothing durable records an offset, and the storage boundary takes no offsets — while the hot-path argument for UTF-16 stands unopposed. Opacity keeps the door open at very low cost.

**The invariant, which every option needs equally:** no position may fall inside a character. In UTF-16 that means never between surrogates; in bytes it would mean never mid-sequence. Cheap to assert, and worth asserting at construction rather than discovering at a render.
