content:
I'll start by catching up on the current state of the protocol.
I've read the protocol through — v1 as-built, `goal/todo.md` and `solution/todo.md`, the milestones backlog, `precedent.md`, R19, and the standing rules in `notes.md`. Then `notes/04 events.md`. Here's where I think this sits, laid out in current terms before I propose anything.

## The gate this has to pass, which is unusually explicit

R19 is one of the few requirements in this project with a written promotion test attached: *"the requirement asks for no date arithmetic, no reminders, no calendar view. If R18 exists, R19 is already satisfied. Anything beyond that must be earned by use."* And `notes.md` records that this project has already been burned once on exactly this question — the events calendar was attributed to era 2 (the excellent one) when it actually came from era 3 (the failed one), which inverted the conclusion, because era 3's version was an Excel sheet and therefore evidence for *less* machinery.

So `notes/04 events.md` is a promotion request against a gate that was deliberately set high, and the strongest thing you can put in front of it is not a design — it's the record of what the pinned file actually failed to do in months of daily use. I'd like that before anything else, and I'll ask for it concretely below.

## The note is not one feature — it's four, with very different evidence behind them

This is why "events" is a bad name: the word is covering things with different shapes, different homes, and different incumbents.

**(A) Task-shaped recurrence.** Air filters, the SA-512 after the normal service. These generate work. Their incumbent is the TODO list plus your memory.

**(B) Event-shaped commitments.** The conference, the birthday, the holiday. These happen whether or not you act, and some of them imply prep. Their incumbent is *Google Calendar*, and R19 says explicitly that Tephra complements it and does not replace it. Most of the machinery in your "how we might represent this" section — date spans, ICS, third-Thursday-of-November, fixed dates by the Hebrew calendar — is a reimplementation of something you already run, correctly, on both devices.

**(C) The horizon.** The compact sidebar strip and the deep view. This is a *surface*, and it's the only part with no incumbent at all.

**(D) The reorient flow.** A rework of the walk. This needs no event machinery whatsoever and could ship first.

Splitting them matters because (B) has to win an argument against Google Calendar that (A), (C) and (D) don't have to fight.

## The reframe I'd like you to argue with

I think the actual missing primitive is much smaller than the note, and it isn't a calendar.

**The TODO list has no way to say "this becomes my problem later."** Every item is present-tense from the moment it exists: it's carried forward every day, it's in the walk every day, it counts against T12's cap every day. A due date surfaces an item but doesn't defer it — an item you create today for November sits on your list for eight weeks doing nothing but making the list longer. That's precisely the accumulation failure era 2 died of, and it's why you currently *can't* write the future down, which is why you're carrying it in your head, which is the thing the success criterion in `goal/todo.md` forbids.

So: **an item gains a wake date alongside its due date.** Dormant until D, then live. One more inline marker in a line, in a notation that already exists.

And then look at what that dissolves. The air filter is not a rule in a separate file that mints a series of items — **it is one item that has been done nine times.** Its id persists; the day-file history already records every time it was done, for free (`solution/todo.md` §6); "every N days from the last time it actually happened" is arithmetic over data you're already keeping. The SA-512 case is the same shape: completing item X wakes item Y, which is a narrow completion-trigger rather than the general item cross-referencing `goal/todo.md` ruled out on twenty years of evidence.

If that holds, class (A) needs **no new file type, no new view, no YAML, and no separate document kind.** What's left in an events file is then only class (B) — things that happen to you rather than things you do — and *that* is much closer to R19's plain table, with one genuinely new field: the ramp-up window.

Which points at the sharpest thing in your note, and I don't think you gave it enough credit: **Tephra doesn't need to know when your wife's birthday is. It needs to know that six weeks beforehand, "think about a present" becomes a live task.** The date is an *input to a rule*; Google Calendar already owns dates and is good at them. The ramp-up window is the invention here, and it's the one thing nothing else in your life does.

## Three collisions worth naming now, not resolving

- **The counting rule.** `scope.md` is three view types, and it's been held. A `.events` directory of YAML would be a fourth kind and the horizon a fourth type. There's an existing mechanism that might absorb it instead: the link directory is D9's filtered-view pattern — an index, a read-only pane, one query — and a horizon has exactly that shape. Whether that's honest or a dodge is worth deciding deliberately rather than by default.
- **YAML.** `scope.md` says one syntax family, leniently parsed markdown, "so a plain reader finds it sensible." A YAML+ICS document breaks that for the first time. Might be right; shouldn't be incidental.
- **What can't be backfilled.** By the standing rule, the question that decides what must ship *now* even if everything else waits is: what data would a later mechanism need that we aren't recording today? My candidates are the wake-date marker and **provenance** — which item was minted by which rule. Without provenance from day one, you can never later tell a generated item from a typed one, and every rule-driven mechanism is retrofitting onto a year of anonymous lines. Same class of hazard as item ids.

## Naming

Your own word is the good one, and I'd split the noun rather than find a single better one: the store is a set of **schedules**; the surface is the **horizon**. That dissolves the naming problem, because the thing you were trying to name was two things.

---

## What I need from you

1. **What actually got missed, in the last few months?** Specific incidents. This is the promotion evidence and it does more work than any argument — and per the record, "urgently need" has to be checked against what actually failed, because era 2 *stored* due dates and missed them anyway.

2. **Which of your five classes are in Google Calendar today, and what does it fail to do for them?** My guess is: it tells you on the day rather than six weeks out, and it has nowhere to put prep tasks. If that's the whole gap, the feature is much smaller than the note.

3. **Does the wake-date reframe hold?** Is the air filter one recurring item with a long history, or a series of separate items? Your intuition here decides whether class (A) is a TODO feature or a new document kind.

4. **Do holidays belong in Tephra at all?** You flagged them as "sort of different" yourself. Under the admission test — what does a holiday in the sidebar beat? — I can't tell whether the answer is real or whether the sidebar strip is looking for content to justify itself.

5. **The walk is "a stub."** The record disagrees — MT5a was designed carefully and shipped. What specifically fell short in use? That's a recorded failure of a shipped feature and I want it precisely, because it's the strongest input to (D), and (D) may be the piece worth building first.

6. **The deep horizon view — would you browse it, or glance at it?** If the compact strip is where all the value is, the table view is a want rather than a need, and saying so early keeps the counting rule intact.

Once we've settled this I'd write it up as `goal/horizon.md`, a sibling to `goal/todo.md`, rather than amending R19 in place — the same move that document made, and for the same reason.
Those are great questions, and my answer is long enough that I just put it into a new section at the end of `notes/04 events.md`.

content:
Read it. The answers move the shape of this materially, and one of them moves it more than the rest.

Let me record the durable part first, since it crosses phases:
## The biggest thing in your answer isn't about events

*"The collection of all related items is itself an artifact that I need to work on, develop, and maintain jointly with my wife: we sit together looking at this list, decide which things to prioritize and act on, when to schedule them, who owns what."*

Two separate things are in that sentence and neither is a date.

**First, it's era 1's failure 3, verbatim.** *"No way to represent a project with its own milestones, so no way to see the list of projects or their status."* Refinishing the floors is not a recurring task or an event with a run-up — it's a project with structure, and the thing you want to look at is the *set*. `goal/todo.md` deliberately split that off as the graveyard problem and said so plainly, and the record notes that splitting it *"let the TODO design get sharp."* It has arrived inside the events feature. I'd resist letting it stay there for exactly the reason it was split off the first time.

**Second — and this is new to the whole project — there's a second person.** Your constraints read *"two devices, both trusted, single user. No multi-tenancy, no sharing model."* And now the hottest item is a list co-owned with your wife, and the era-3 spreadsheet turns out to have been co-owned with an exec assistant: *"it was a communication channel with someone who helped me plan and manage things."* That's two of your three strongest wants being **shared surfaces**, and the record never had that input.

I've written both to `notes.md` so they don't get lost in this feature.

I want to be careful not to inflate it, though, because there's a cheap version and an expensive one and they look identical in the sentence you wrote. **Does she need *access*, or does she need to be *in the room while you both look at one screen*?** The first is a multi-user product with sync, identity and permissions — categorically outside this project. The second is "a table that two people can read at once," which costs nothing and which you'd want anyway. My read of "we sit together looking at this list" is that it's the second, and that "who owns what" is a column, not an account. If that's right, this collapses almost entirely, and D46's lesson applies — the boundary moves out to a coarser container and the propagation disappears.

## What the evidence confirmed, and what it killed

**The horizon view is a need, not a want — and you handed me the gate's answer.** *"I really want this view to exist again."* Note what's underneath it: R18 shipped months ago. You have pinned lists. You could have made that table as a pinned markdown file on any day since, and you didn't. Per this project's own discipline, that's a gate that was *opened* and returned an actual negative — which is far better evidence than the argument in the first half of your note. The question it raises is the useful one: **what does a plain markdown table lack that Excel had?** My candidates are that it doesn't sort itself by date, doesn't retire past events, doesn't connect to the task list, and — most likely the real one — nothing ever shows it to you, so it doesn't get maintained. If that last one dominates, then the compact strip isn't decoration around the view; it's what keeps the view alive.

**Run-up awareness is confirmed, and the talk case states it most precisely:** *"the most important thing is that during that window, I'm aware that a talk is approaching and am thinking about it during downtime."* That is an **awareness** requirement, not a task requirement, and it's the one thing the TODO list structurally cannot express — an item is a thing to do, not a state to be in. So your "reminder with no TODO" category is real after all. Just not for the reason you first gave: holidays don't need it, *the run-up state itself* does.

**Holidays are settled and got cheaper.** Only on the calendar, but useful as rows in the horizon. That's read-only, and it means Tephra never needs to know what a Jewish holiday is — it needs to be able to display dated rows that came from somewhere else.

**Trip templates are a fifth thing, and possibly the cheapest big win.** *"I literally do have a doc template for the details of a trip."* Instantiating a template into a doc plus a bundle of tasks is an old, well-understood mechanism with no date arithmetic in it at all. It's orthogonal to everything else here and I'd hold it separate.

## Where I'd now put the pieces

| | Evidence | Where it belongs |
|---|---|---|
| **The horizon** (list of major events, incl. holidays) | Strongest — had it, lost it, gate returned a negative | R19's promotion. A view + a plain table. |
| **Run-up windows** (talks, trips, birthday) | Strong — "had to remember by hand" | New. The one genuine invention. |
| **Recurring maintenance** (filters, car) | Strong — "simply terrible at remembering" | A TODO feature, if the wake-date reframe holds |
| **Household projects + joint list** | Hottest, and years of failed tools | **Its own clarification.** Not this. |
| **Trip templates** | Real, and you already have the template | Separate, orthogonal, cheap |

The line I'd draw: **everything in this feature ends up as a TODO item or a horizon row.** You said the thing that makes Tephra work here yourself — *"it's already a dashboard that I look at daily... if something shows up on 'I need to do this today' then it's now in my head."* That's the delivery mechanism for all of it, and it means the schedules file is a *generator*, with no surface of its own. Which is a much smaller feature than the note's middle section describes.

## One collision your answer created

You now imply traffic in **both directions** with Google Calendar: holidays read *in* to the horizon, and trips generating calendar items that *"should naturally surface on my existing (Google) calendar."*

The read direction is nearly free if it's an **ICS file** dropped in the directory — which your own note already proposed. That's a file, so R25, R26 and offline operation all survive untouched.

The write direction is a different animal: it's OAuth, a network dependency, tokens, and the first time Tephra talks to a service. This app has never done that, and `notes.md` carries a specific rule about which kinds of dependency are acceptable. **Did you mean Tephra should create those calendar entries, or just that trips have calendar entries and those live on Google Calendar?** If it's the latter, the whole problem evaporates.

## Still open, and small

1. **The wake-date reframe** — is the air filter one recurring item with a long history, or a fresh item each time? Your answer decides whether recurring maintenance is a two-line addition to the TODO format or a new document kind.
2. **The walk being "a stub."** Still unanswered, and your reorient flow rests entirely on it. MT5a was designed carefully and shipped; what specifically fell short in use is a recorded failure of a shipped feature, and it's the best input to the one piece of this that needs no event machinery at all.

Answer those two plus the calendar direction and I'll write `goal/horizon.md`. The household/projects thread I'd hold for its own clarification — probably the one to run *next*, given you called it the hottest thing on your list.

The cheap version is the one I intended: We need to sit in the same room next to each other, looking at the screen while we discuss. We don’t need a multi-user project for this.

One thing I would point out: The set of “all household tasks, either recurring maintenance or projects that have to be done” is the thing that my wife and I need to look at and discuss together. Really, each of the individual event files I proposed in the notes has this property: these are logical groupings of events or tasks which need to be reasoned about and edited as a group, and that’s an important UX affordance. 

I do agree that TODO items and horizon rows are the two delivery mechanisms; the edit experience that combines things in this logical way is the third experience that fills this out.

I don’t think we need write from Tephra to Google Calendar at this point. I’d rather manage trips separately and manually add them than do major feature bloat just to support that.

The walk being a stub is really a statement about how we didn’t fully understand its significance as a UI action — it’s not about “groom the TODO list,” it’s about “refresh my own mental state, and ensure that the TODO list, horizon view, etc., and my own cognitive state all align.” That makes this flow much more of a central aspect of our design.

# The Horizon

**Scope: knowing what is coming, and having it arrive as work in time to do it.** This promotes R19, which held the events calendar to a pinned markdown file and set an explicit gate — *"the requirement asks for no date arithmetic, no reminders, no calendar view... anything beyond that must be earned by use."* The gate has now been opened and has returned a negative; the evidence is below.

**Not in scope: the project with its own milestones.** Refinishing the floors is not a recurring task or a dated event, and it arrived here only because the household case needs both. That is era 1's third failure and the graveyard problem, and it wants its own clarification (`notes.md`). The distinction that keeps them apart: **this design is the container; a project is a possible member shape.** Birthdays need the container and no projects.

## What the record says

**Era 3's events spreadsheet is the one thing in era 3 that worked** (`precedent.md`) — major commitments only, each with a date or range, location, summary, contact, in Excel, with no ceremony. R19 was derived from it correctly and concluded that a plain table kept separate was the whole requirement.

**Two things have changed since, and both are evidence rather than argument.**

**The gate was opened and it failed.** R18 shipped months ago; pinned lists exist; a markdown table could have been made on any day since, and was not. Per this project's own discipline a gate that was never opened has not returned a negative — but this one *was*, and it did. What a plain file lacks is not storage. It does not order itself, does not retire what has passed, does not reach the task list, and **nothing ever shows it to you, so it does not get maintained.** The surfacing is the feature; the table is the cheap part. That is the same finding T9 recorded about due dates — era 2 stored them and missed them anyway.

**The spreadsheet was co-owned.** It ran alongside a full-time exec assistant and was *"a communication channel with someone who helped me plan and manage things."* So part of what made it work was that it was a surface two people looked at. That property is live today in a different form (below) and was invisible in R19's derivation.

**And what is being missed is recorded plainly.** Household maintenance that recurs and is *"simply terrible at remembering."* Trips, talks and a wife's birthday, all of which need weeks or months of run-up, and every one of which *"anything tied to remembering these, I've had to remember, and generate the corresponding TODO items for, by hand."*

## Three surfaces, and the third is the source

The delivery mechanisms are the two that already exist or nearly do — a **TODO item** and a **horizon row**. What was missing from the first reading of this problem is a third thing, and it is where the truth lives:

| | Holds | Bounded by | Turnover |
|---|---|---|---|
| **The TODO list** | what is in front of me now | a soft cap (T12) | daily |
| **The horizon** | what is coming soon | a time window | continuous |
| **A schedule** | everything true about one domain | nothing — it is complete | indefinite |

**Completeness is the property that distinguishes a schedule**, and it is what earns the right to stop carrying a house in your head. The TODO list is emphatically not complete — its whole design is about what is in front of you — and the horizon is not either. A schedule is, for its domain, and it therefore holds things that are dormant, not yet started, or merely standing.

**A schedule is not a tag pivot.** The pivot shows live items under a tag; a schedule's contents are mostly not live and many will never become TODO items at all.

## A schedule is edited as a group, sitting next to someone

**This is a first-class motion, not a file-management convenience.** *"We sit together looking at this list, decide which things to prioritize and act on, when to schedule them, who owns what."* Each grouping the user proposed — household tasks per house, birthdays, holidays, speaking engagements — is a set that gets reasoned about and revised as a whole.

**And it needs no sharing model.** The requirement is two people in one room reading one screen, not two people with accounts. That is a **legibility** requirement on the view — readable at conversational distance, navigable while talking — and in this project legibility requirements are hard requirements. The single-user constraint in `requirements.md` stands untouched, and *"who owns what"* is a column, not an identity.

## What reorient actually is

**The walk was scoped to one document, and its job is scoped to a whole situation.** `goal/todo.md` had already found half of this — the walk is not garbage collection, its output is attention — but it kept the scope at the task list. The correction: reorient is *"refresh my own mental state, and ensure that the TODO list, horizon view, and my own cognitive state all align."*

**That inverts this design.** Reorient is not one flow among several; it is what every other mechanism here feeds. The horizon exists to have something to show at reorient. The ramp-up window exists so the right things are in it. Schedules exist so nothing is missing from what it can reach. It is invocable on demand — whenever the state has got away from you — and offered on the day boundary, which is where the walk already hangs (D62).

**One structural constraint follows immediately, and it is the TODO design's own rule repeated.** There the **carry** is automatic and protects the data, while the **walk** is offered and protects the attention. Here: **generation is automatic and must never be contingent on reorient.** A ramp-up window that fires only when you sit down means three skipped days are three unfired windows — and where a skipped walk cost a day's grooming, a skipped reorient would cost the talk. Reorient may only ever *show* you what has already happened.

## The tension, and the one thing that reconciles it

A schedule must be **complete**, or something falls out of it and dies unseen. The horizon must be **short**, or it stops being read and you are blind anyway. Those pull directly against each other, and this is the same shape as T11 against T12.

**The reconciler is the ramp-up window, and that is why it is the real invention here.** It is not a reminder setting; it is the per-entry parameter that decides what reaches the horizon *at all*, and it is what lets a complete record project onto a readable surface. A talk wants two weeks. A wife's birthday wants a few months, because the output is *"sitting down and creating a doc just to figure out the plan."* An air filter wants a few days. A global setting cannot express that, so **the window is authored per entry**.

This also settles a category the first reading dismissed. *"The most important thing is that during that window, I'm aware that a talk is approaching and am thinking about it during downtime."* That is an **awareness state**, not a task, and the TODO list cannot express it — an item is a thing to do. So "a reminder with no TODO" is real, not for holidays but for the run-up itself.

## Requirements

**H1. Three surfaces over one source.** A schedule is the durable record; TODO items and horizon rows are projections of it. Nothing is authored twice, and no projection is the place where something is remembered.

**H2. A schedule is complete about its domain**, and holds entries that are dormant, standing, or not yet live. This is what distinguishes it from the capped working list and the windowed horizon.

**H3. A schedule is edited as a group.** Reasoning about the set is a first-class motion, performed beside another person reading the same screen. Legibility at conversational distance is a requirement on this view, not polish. **No sharing model, no accounts, no multi-user anything** — the constraint in `requirements.md` is untouched.

**H4. Every entry carries a ramp-up window**, authored per entry, which decides when it becomes live. This is what reconciles H2 with H8.

**H5. Entries generate TODO items** — templated text with substitution from the occurrence, tags, and a due date. Generation is **automatic, on the day boundary, and never contingent on reorient** (H10).

**H6. An entry may generate awareness with no task.** The run-up state is a thing to be in, which no TODO item can express.

**H7. Recurrence covers one-off, an explicit list, a pointer to an ICS file, and *N days after the last time it actually happened*.** The last requires recording when it happened, and therefore requires marking which item completes the entry. Calendar-rule recurrence — Hebrew dates, third Thursday of November — is wanted later and not now.

**H8. The compact horizon is always present** in the ordinary working view, short by construction, and shows what is happening now or imminently.

**H9. The full horizon is era 3's spreadsheet, restored** — every major commitment across every schedule in one date-ordered list, including holidays. **This is not a calendar view**: a calendar answers *what am I doing on day X* and is full of meetings; this answers *what is coming*, and is a list.

**H10. Generation is automatic; reorient is offered.** A skipped reorient costs the day's attention and never the data. This is the carry/walk split, repeated because the cost of getting it wrong is higher here.

**H11. Reorient spans the whole situation** — the task list, the horizon, and what is standing — and is invocable on demand as well as offered at the day boundary. It supersedes T11, which was the same flow scoped to one document.

**H12. Dated rows may be read from an ICS file kept in the notebook.** A file, not a service: holidays belong on the calendar and appear here as rows. **Tephra never writes to an external calendar** — trips are entered there by hand, which is deliberately preferred over the feature bloat of an integration.

**H13. A generated item records what generated it.** Provenance cannot be backfilled: without it, no later mechanism can ever tell a generated line from a typed one. Same class of hazard as item ids and R15's timestamps, and therefore the part that must ship first even if the rest waits.

**H14. Entries carry an optional link to one document and an optional owner.** Both derived from experience rather than from analysis.

**H15. Schedules are plain, legible, hand-editable files** (R26, carried), and remain sensible to a reader who does not have Tephra.

## Success

**"I know what is coming, nothing that arrives is a surprise, and I am carrying none of it in my head."**

Two failure modes, pulling opposite ways — the same structure as `goal/todo.md`'s, and the reason that document's tension was the substance of its problem:

- **Blindness** — something arrives that should have been seen coming. Guarded by H2 (the record is complete) and H5 (it fires whether or not anyone looks).
- **Noise** — the horizon fills, stops being read, and blindness returns through the front door. Guarded by H4, the only mechanism here that can shorten the horizon without shortening the record.

A design that optimizes either alone fails.

## What is invented rather than derived

Three things go past the evidence and should be argued with. **The ramp-up window as a per-entry parameter** — the need for run-up is well evidenced, that this is its shape is not. **Reorient as the design's centre** rather than as one flow among several; it is a reframe offered in conversation and has not been lived with. And **the schedule as a document kind** — the group-editing motion is real and evidenced, but that it wants a kind of its own rather than a mode of something existing is a choice, and Qb below is where it gets tested.

## Open

**Qa. Is a recurring task one item that comes back, or a series of minted items?** If one, its id persists, its day-file history *is* the record of every time it was done, "N days since it last happened" is free, and H7 costs a wake-date marker in the TODO format. If a series, recurrence needs machinery of its own. This decides how much of H5 and H7 is a TODO feature versus a new one, and it is the largest unforced question here.

**Qb. Is the horizon a fourth view type?** `scope.md`'s counting rule is three and has held. There is an existing mechanism that may absorb it: the link directory is D9's filtered-view pattern — an index, a read-only pane, one query — and the horizon has that shape exactly. Whether that is honest or a dodge should be decided deliberately.

**Qc. What is a schedule's syntax?** The note proposes YAML, which would be the first break in `scope.md`'s one-syntax-family rule. That rule exists for merge safety and for the plain reader, and breaking it may be right; it should not happen by default.

**Qd. What is reorient's actual sequence?** H11 says what it spans and not what it does. It is now load-bearing for four mechanisms, so it needs designing rather than accreting.

## Decisions and requirements this revisits

- **R19 is promoted**, against the evidence its own gate demanded. What it got right survives: the full horizon is a plain date-ordered list, not a calendar view.
- **T11 is superseded by H11.** Same ritual, wrong scope.
- **The single-user constraint is confirmed, and cheaply.** Two people, one screen. Recorded here because the question was live and the answer forecloses a large branch.
- **`goal/todo.md`'s ban on items referencing each other is narrowly breached** by H7's completion-relative recurrence and by *"schedule the SA-512 maintenance after the normal service."* The ban rests on twenty years of evidence that general cross-reference is low value; what is needed is only *completion of X wakes Y*, which is the same mechanism as completion-relative recurrence and does not reopen the general case.
- **`scope.md`'s counting rule is at stake** — see Qb.

Four answers, and two of them change the design's shape. Let me take the correction first, because I got it wrong last turn.

**I over-split.** I decomposed by *delivery* — TODO item or horizon row — and concluded the schedules file was "a generator with no surface of its own." You're right that this drops an axis. The group is itself an object you reason about and edit as a unit, and that's not a pivot over the task list: the tag pivot shows what's *live now*, and the household set has to show the dormant, the not-yet-started and the merely standing. A tag pivot is a view over the TODO list; a schedule contains things that aren't TODO items yet and may never be.

So there are three surfaces, and the third is the source:

- **The TODO list** — what's in front of me *now*. Capped, daily, transient.
- **The horizon** — what's coming *soon*. Windowed by time.
- **A schedule** — everything true about one domain, indefinitely. **Complete**, durable, edited as a group.

Completeness is the property that distinguishes it, and it's what makes it safe to stop carrying the house in your head. The other two are projections of it.

But the split I made *does* survive in a narrower form, and it's cleaner now: a schedule is a **container**; a project with milestones is a possible **member shape**. Birthdays need the container and no projects. The household needs both, which is why it read as one thing. The container is this feature; the project is still the graveyard problem.

## Reorient inverts the design

Your reframe is the other big one, and it retroactively explains something already in the record. `goal/todo.md` had found half of it — *"the walk is not garbage collection... its output is attention"* — and `notes.md` carries the general lesson about a ritual having a job other than the one it looks like. What you've added is that **its scope was wrong.** It was scoped to one document; the job is scoped to your whole situation. Loading the list into your head is a subroutine of loading your circumstances into your head.

That inverts the note's structure. Reorient isn't the third UX flow after the horizon views — **it's the thing every other mechanism here is feeding.** The horizon exists to have something to show at reorient; the ramp-up window exists so the right things are in it; the schedules exist so nothing is missing from what it can reach.

And it forces one hard constraint, by direct application of a rule this project already paid for. The TODO design splits **carry** (automatic, protects the data) from **walk** (offered, protects the attention). That split has to be repeated: **generation must be automatic and must never be contingent on reorient.** Your note has the morning routine "including the day's reminders," which reads as the routine producing them — and if it does, skipping three days means three unfired ramp-ups. When the walk only groomed, a lapse cost grooming. If reorient is where you learn a talk is in two weeks, a lapse costs the talk.

Let me write this up.
Written to `.clarity-protocol/goal/horizon.md`, as a sibling to `goal/todo.md` and in the same shape. R19 is amended in place to point at it, and `notes.md` carries the household/second-person finding for the graveyard clarification.

**What's in it, in brief.** Fifteen requirements (H1–H15) around three surfaces over one source; the completeness-versus-noise tension and the ramp-up window as the only thing that reconciles it; reorient as the design's centre with the automatic/offered split made explicit; and the success criterion — *"I know what is coming, nothing that arrives is a surprise, and I am carrying none of it in my head"* — decomposed into blindness and noise, which pull opposite ways.

**Three things I flagged as invented rather than derived**, since you'll want to argue with them specifically: the ramp-up window as a per-entry parameter (the *need* for run-up is well evidenced; that this is its shape is not), reorient as the centre (a reframe from conversation, not yet lived with), and the schedule as a document kind of its own rather than a mode of something existing.

**Four open questions**, and the first is the one you haven't answered yet:

- **Qa — is a recurring task one item that comes back, or a series of minted items?** This is the largest unforced question here. If it's one item, its id persists, the day-file history *is* the record of every time it was done, "N days since it last happened" is free, and H7 costs one wake-date marker in the TODO format. If it's a series, recurrence needs machinery of its own. Your answer decides how much of this is a TODO feature versus a new one.
- **Qb — is the horizon a fourth view type?** The counting rule has held at three. The link directory is the precedent that might absorb it: index, read-only pane, one query — the horizon has that shape exactly.
- **Qc — schedule syntax.** YAML would be the first break in the one-syntax-family rule, which exists for merge safety and for the plain reader. Might be right; shouldn't happen by default.
- **Qd — reorient's actual sequence.** H11 says what it spans, not what it does, and it's now load-bearing for four mechanisms.

**Two things I'd suggest doing next, in this order.** Qa first — it's cheap to answer, it's the only one that changes how much of this is new code, and it's a representation question you can settle by asking what you'd want to *see* when you look at the air filter. Then the household/projects clarification, since you called it the hottest thing on your list and it's now cleanly separated: the container is this design, the project is still unstarted.

One naming note — I used **schedule** for the document kind (your own word: *"does it happen on a schedule?"*), **horizon** for the view, and **reorient** for the flow. "The household schedule" and "the speaking engagements schedule" both read naturally; "the birthdays schedule" is slightly odd. Easy to change now and annoying later, so worth a moment.

Qb: This definitely smells like a fourth view type. Not surprising; if you have 3 of something, you’ll end up with N.

content:
Four good answers. Let me record the two that are settled, then take up names and reorient.
Qa and Qb are recorded, with what they force. Two notes on Qa before moving on: because occurrences are independent, **completion has to flow backward** — the entry can't recover "when did it last happen" from an item's history, so provenance is now a two-way channel rather than a diagnostic. And **an entry has to know whether it has an occurrence outstanding**, or a filter task you never complete either duplicates every cycle or silently stops recurring. Accumulation or a graveyard.

## Names

You've probably noticed I already leaned on one above. Here's the argument.

**The strongest reason to move off "schedule" and "event" isn't that they're bland — it's that each burns a word we need elsewhere.** Every entry *has* a recurrence schedule, so the type can't also be "schedule" without producing "the schedule of an entry in a schedule." And "event" has to stay available as an ordinary word — *the day the event happens* — which it can't if it's a type name. A name that forecloses vocabulary you need one layer down is a bad name regardless of how it reads.

Two constraints on the inner noun: **"item" is taken** by TODO, and **"entry" is semi-taken** by filesets.

And one thing that lowers the stakes: **the kind name mostly lives in the extension and the design docs, not in your speech.** You say "Sections," the kind is `fileset`. You'd say "the house list," the file is `house.docket`. So an instance that reads slightly oddly against the kind name is tolerable.

| pair | reads | for | against |
|---|---|---|---|
| **docket / matter** | *the household docket; nine matters on it* | A docket is a complete list of things awaiting attention, in date order, actively worked — and it's the thing a judge and clerk look at *together*. "Matter" is deliberately vague between task and event, which is the ambiguity we actually need. Pairs beautifully with horizon: **the docket is everything; the horizon is its near end.** | Legal register. "The birthdays docket" is dry. |
| **almanac / entry** | *the household almanac* | Literally the genre: recurring dated things, holidays, and when to do the seasonal chores. Warm, and on this project's register — Tephra, the Aldine page, the Talmudic margin. | Connotes *reference* — fixed, published, read-only — which fights H3's "edited as a group." And "entry" collides with filesets. |
| **register / commitment** | *the register of speaking engagements* | "Register" carries **completeness** exactly, which is H2. | Clerical, and badly overloaded in software. |
| **slate / fixture** | *the household slate* | Short; "fixture" has a nice double meaning for a house. | Reads as sports throughout. |

**I'd take docket / matter**, mostly on the horizon pairing and on "matter" being the only candidate that's honestly indifferent between a task and an event. Almanac is the one I'd switch to if you want warmth over precision — it's the better *word* and the worse *fit*.

## Reorient

Here's a proposal to react to rather than a menu.

**The finding that separates it from the walk: reorient has an output.** The walk's output was attention and nothing else — it wrote only what you changed. But you named the goal as ending with *"which items I've decided to do today,"* and that's an artifact. So reorient isn't review, it's **selection**: it starts from everything live and ends with a short designated set. That's also why the same flow serves both invocations. After one day little has moved and it's fast; after three weeks the middle is long and the selection is a real reduction. **The cost is proportional to what's changed, not to what exists** — which is the walk's "defaults to unchanged" principle, extended.

**Three movements, and the order has a reason:**

1. **What's coming.** The horizon first, because it's *context for the selection*. Whether a task matters today depends on whether there's a talk in ten days. Read the list first and discover the talk afterward, and you have to redo the choosing. Usually a few rows.
2. **What's live.** MT5a exactly as built — every item, defaults to unchanged, drop staged. The long movement, and the only one whose length varies much.
3. **What's today.** Choose from what you just looked at. This is what you leave with.

**Dockets are not walked.** A docket is complete and mostly dormant; stepping through hundreds of standing entries daily is absurd, and its real review rhythm is you and your wife sitting down occasionally. So reorient sees the *projections*, not the contents — which is just H1 holding. But it should surface **docket staleness**: one line, *"household — not reviewed since June."* A complete record nobody opens isn't protective, and that's the graveyard risk arriving inside the mechanism built to prevent it.

**What makes a skipped reorient safe.** Generation being automatic (H10) protects the data, but there's a second exposure: a talk-in-two-weeks task is one line in a long list, and the *awareness state* H6 exists for never reaches your head. The guard is the compact horizon — always present in the ordinary working view, whether or not anyone reorients. So **the compact horizon isn't a convenience; it's what makes a skipped reorient safe**, precisely as the walk is what makes the soft cap safe. Two features that each look optional, one mechanism with two halves.

**And one question I'd rather ask than answer.** If reorient produces a chosen today-set, what happens to MT5c, the soft cap? A cap truncates arbitrarily; a selection chooses meaningfully — so the today-set appears to replace the cap's *visibility* half outright. But Q3 established the cap had two jobs, and the other one was **entry cost**: an item you know you won't see is one you think twice about writing. A today-set doesn't obviously produce that pressure. My instinct is that they aren't substitutes and the today-set changes what the cap should be counting, but I'd rather have your read — Q3 is the one place this project has already been wrong about a mechanism doing two jobs at once.

Tell me where this lands and I'll write reorient into the doc as H11's design rather than its scope.

I love docket and matter! My wife already jokes that I have a dedicated “docket face” which is my expression when reading over legal dockets, this will make a great in-joke between us.

I also love your perspective on reorientation, that feels very correct. I think the entire “soft cap” concept is one that we can safely punt for the moment: I want to see how the system works in practice more, especially with this in place, before thinking about what we really need there. 

The today set is tied to something I found myself doing in era 3 when I had a lot of items on the list: during the walkthrough I would create a special “today” section and move various items into it, essentially deciding on how I was going to structure my day right there and then. It was a really useful attention-focusing mechanism during busy periods.

# The Horizon

**Scope: knowing what is coming, and having it arrive as work in time to do it.** This promotes R19, which held the events calendar to a pinned markdown file and set an explicit gate — *"the requirement asks for no date arithmetic, no reminders, no calendar view... anything beyond that must be earned by use."* The gate has now been opened and has returned a negative; the evidence is below.

**Not in scope: the project with its own milestones.** Refinishing the floors is not a recurring task or a dated event, and it arrived here only because the household case needs both. That is era 1's third failure and the graveyard problem, and it wants its own clarification (`notes.md`). The distinction that keeps them apart: **this design is the container; a project is a possible member shape.** Birthdays need the container and no projects.

## The vocabulary

Four things, and the names were chosen rather than defaulted.

- **A docket** — the document kind. A complete, durable set of standing commitments in one domain: a house, birthdays, holidays, speaking engagements.
- **A matter** — one thing on a docket. Deliberately indifferent between a task and an event, because half of them are each.
- **The horizon** — the view over every docket. The docket is everything; the horizon is its near end.
- **Reorient** — the flow that makes your picture of all this agree with the system's.

**"Schedule" and "event" were rejected for a specific reason**, not for taste: each burns a word needed one layer down. Every matter *has* a recurrence schedule, and "event" must stay available as an ordinary word — *the day the event happens*. A type name that forecloses vocabulary beneath it is a bad type name however well it reads. *(Also: **item** belongs to TODO and **entry** to filesets, which is why the inner noun is neither.)*

## What the record says

**Era 3's events spreadsheet is the one thing in era 3 that worked** (`precedent.md`) — major commitments only, each with a date or range, location, summary, contact, in Excel, with no ceremony. R19 was derived from it correctly and concluded that a plain table kept separate was the whole requirement.

**Two things have changed since, and both are evidence rather than argument.**

**The gate was opened and it failed.** R18 shipped months ago; pinned lists exist; a markdown table could have been made on any day since, and was not. Per this project's own discipline a gate that was never opened has not returned a negative — but this one *was*, and it did. What a plain file lacks is not storage. It does not order itself, does not retire what has passed, does not reach the task list, and **nothing ever shows it to you, so it does not get maintained.** The surfacing is the feature; the table is the cheap part. That is the same finding T9 recorded about due dates — era 2 stored them and missed them anyway.

**The spreadsheet was co-owned.** It ran alongside a full-time exec assistant and was *"a communication channel with someone who helped me plan and manage things."* So part of what made it work was that it was a surface two people looked at. That property is live today in a different form (H3) and was invisible in R19's derivation.

**And what is being missed is recorded plainly.** Household maintenance that recurs and is *"simply terrible at remembering."* Trips, talks and a wife's birthday, all needing weeks or months of run-up, and every one of which *"anything tied to remembering these, I've had to remember, and generate the corresponding TODO items for, by hand."*

## Three surfaces, and the third is the source

The delivery mechanisms are the two that already exist or nearly do — a **TODO item** and a **horizon row**. What was missing from the first reading of this problem is a third thing, and it is where the truth lives:

| | Holds | Bounded by | Turnover |
|---|---|---|---|
| **The TODO list** | what is in front of me now | today's selection (H9) | daily |
| **The horizon** | what is coming soon | a time window | continuous |
| **A docket** | everything true about one domain | nothing — it is complete | indefinite |

**Completeness is the property that distinguishes a docket**, and it is what earns the right to stop carrying a house in your head. The TODO list is emphatically not complete — its whole design is about what is in front of you — and the horizon is not either. A docket is, for its domain, and it therefore holds matters that are dormant, not yet started, or merely standing.

**A docket is not a tag pivot.** The pivot shows live items under a tag; a docket's contents are mostly not live and many will never become TODO items at all.

## A docket is edited as a group, sitting next to someone

**This is a first-class motion, not a file-management convenience.** *"We sit together looking at this list, decide which things to prioritize and act on, when to schedule them, who owns what."* Each grouping the user proposed — household matters per house, birthdays, holidays, speaking engagements — is a set that gets reasoned about and revised as a whole.

**And it needs no sharing model.** The requirement is two people in one room reading one screen, not two people with accounts. That is a **legibility** requirement on the view — readable at conversational distance, navigable while talking — and in this project legibility requirements are hard requirements. The single-user constraint in `requirements.md` stands untouched, and *"who owns what"* is a column, not an identity.

## What reorient actually is

**The walk was scoped to one document, and its job is scoped to a whole situation.** `goal/todo.md` had already found half of this — the walk is not garbage collection, its output is attention — but it kept the scope at the task list. The correction: reorient is *"refresh my own mental state, and ensure that the TODO list, horizon view, and my own cognitive state all align."*

**That inverts this design.** Reorient is not one flow among several; it is what every other mechanism here feeds. The horizon exists to have something to show at reorient. The ramp-up window exists so the right things are in it. Dockets exist so nothing is missing from what it can reach.

### It has an output, and that is what separates it from the walk

The walk wrote only what you changed; its product was attention and nothing else. Reorient ends with an artifact — **the day's selection**, the short set you have decided to actually do. So it is not review, it is **selection**: it starts from everything live and ends with something shorter.

**This is derived, not invented.** In era 3, under a tool that offered nothing for it, the user spontaneously *"created a special 'today' section and moved various items into it, essentially deciding how I was going to structure my day right there and then... a really useful attention-focusing mechanism during busy periods."* A practice adopted without a feature to prompt it is the strongest evidence this project recognises.

**And it is very probably the same practice as era 3's "urgent" section** — *"one section for urgent tasks, things that absolutely had to happen today"* (`notes/03`). Same era, same ritual, same position in the list, described twice. If so, **T9's due-soon band and the day's selection are one band**, which matters: two bands stacked above a list is the "scan two ways at once" failure era 2 died of.

**One band, two sources.** Dates arriving push into it **automatically**, because a due date that appears on Wednesday cannot wait for someone to choose to reorient. Your decisions at reorient **curate** it. One place the eye goes; the difference between *the calendar put this here* and *I put this here* is a mark, not a second region.

**A selection, never a relocation.** Era 3 achieved this by moving items into a section, and this design cannot: `goal/todo.md` forbids re-arranging the list, because era 2's nesting could express urgency or subject but never both. The band is where the selection shows; the list underneath is untouched, in creation order, exactly where you know your way around it.

### The three movements

Same flow for the daily pass and for the *"I've been away and I'm overwhelmed"* pass — **its cost is proportional to what has changed, not to what exists**, which is the walk's defaults-to-unchanged principle extended. After a day it is a few gestures; after three weeks the middle is long and the selection is a real reduction.

1. **What's coming** — the horizon. *First*, because it is context for the selection: whether a task matters today depends on whether there is a talk in ten days. Read the list first and discover the talk afterward, and the choosing has to be redone.
2. **What's live** — the walk, exactly as MT5a built it. Every item, defaults to unchanged, drop staged. The long movement.
3. **What's today** — choose from what you have just looked at. The output.

**Dockets are not walked.** A docket is complete and mostly dormant, and stepping through hundreds of standing matters daily is absurd; its real rhythm is two people sitting down with it occasionally. Reorient sees the *projections*, not the contents — which is H1 holding. But it surfaces **docket staleness** in one line — *"household — not reviewed since June"* — because a complete record nobody opens is not protective, and that is the graveyard risk arriving inside the mechanism built to prevent it.

## The tension, and the one thing that reconciles it

A docket must be **complete**, or something falls out of it and dies unseen. The horizon must be **short**, or it stops being read and you are blind anyway. Those pull directly against each other, and this is the same shape as T11 against T12.

**The reconciler is the ramp-up window, and that is why it is the real invention here.** It is not a reminder setting; it is the per-matter parameter deciding what reaches the horizon *at all*, and it is what lets a complete record project onto a readable surface. A talk wants two weeks. A wife's birthday wants a few months, because the output is *"sitting down and creating a doc just to figure out the plan."* An air filter wants a few days. A global setting cannot express that, so **the window is authored per matter**.

This also settles a category the first reading dismissed. *"The most important thing is that during that window, I'm aware that a talk is approaching and am thinking about it during downtime."* That is an **awareness state**, not a task, and the TODO list cannot express it — an item is a thing to do. So "a reminder with no TODO" is real, not for holidays but for the run-up itself.

## Requirements

**H1. Three surfaces over one source.** A docket is the durable record; TODO items and horizon rows are projections of it. Nothing is authored twice, and no projection is the place where something is remembered.

**H2. A docket is complete about its domain**, and holds matters that are dormant, standing, or not yet live. This is what distinguishes it from the working list and the windowed horizon.

**H3. A docket is edited as a group.** Reasoning about the set is a first-class motion, performed beside another person reading the same screen. Legibility at conversational distance is a requirement on this view, not polish. **No sharing model, no accounts, no multi-user anything** — the constraint in `requirements.md` is untouched.

**H4. Every matter carries a ramp-up window**, authored per matter, which decides when it becomes live. This is what reconciles H2 with H8.

**H5. Matters generate TODO items** — templated text with substitution from the occurrence, tags, and a due date. Generation is **automatic, on the day boundary, and never contingent on reorient** (H10).

**H6. A matter may generate awareness with no task.** The run-up state is a thing to be in, which no TODO item can express.

**H7. Recurrence covers one-off, an explicit list, a pointer to an ICS file, and *N days after the last time it actually happened*.** Calendar-rule recurrence — Hebrew dates, third Thursday of November — is wanted later and not now.

**H7a. The matter recurs; the tasks it generates do not.** The air filter is one durable matter with identity and history, and each occurrence mints a **fresh, independent** TODO item that can be edited, retagged, deferred or dropped without touching the recurrence. Two things follow, and neither is optional:

- **Completion flows backward.** Because occurrences are independent, "N days since it last happened" cannot be recovered from an item's own history — the matter has to be told. One generated item per occurrence is designated as the one whose completion advances the clock.
- **A matter knows whether it has an occurrence outstanding.** Otherwise a filter task never completed either generates a duplicate every cycle or silently stops recurring — accumulation or a graveyard, and both are failures this project is named against. An outstanding occurrence is shown as overdue rather than reissued.

**H8. The compact horizon is always present** in the ordinary working view, short by construction. **It is not a convenience: it is what makes a skipped reorient safe.** Generation being automatic protects the data, but the *awareness* H6 exists for would otherwise be one line in a long list and never reach anyone's head. Exactly as the walk is what makes the soft cap safe, this is what makes an optional ritual affordable.

**H9. One band above the list, holding the day's selection**, with two sources: matters and items whose dates have arrived, added automatically; and what you chose at reorient. A mark distinguishes them. It supersedes T9's due-soon band rather than sitting beside it, and it is a **selection, never a relocation** — the list beneath stays in creation order.

**H10. Generation is automatic; reorient is offered.** A skipped reorient costs the day's attention and never the data. This is the carry/walk split, repeated because the cost of getting it wrong is higher here.

**H11. Reorient spans the whole situation** — the horizon, the live list, and the day's selection, in that order — and is invocable on demand as well as offered at the day boundary. It supersedes T11, which was the same flow scoped to one document. It reports docket staleness and does not walk docket contents.

**H12. Dated rows may be read from an ICS file kept in the notebook.** A file, not a service: holidays belong on the calendar and appear here as rows. **Tephra never writes to an external calendar** — trips are entered there by hand, which is deliberately preferred over the feature bloat of an integration.

**H13. A generated item records what generated it.** Provenance cannot be backfilled: without it, no later mechanism can ever tell a generated line from a typed one. Same class of hazard as item ids and R15's timestamps, and therefore the part that must ship first even if the rest waits. **H7a makes it doubly earned** — the link is also the channel completion travels back along, so it is read in both directions and is load-bearing rather than diagnostic.

**H14. Matters carry an optional link to one document and an optional owner.** Both derived from experience rather than from analysis.

**H15. Dockets are plain, legible, hand-editable files** (R26, carried), and remain sensible to a reader who does not have Tephra.

## Success

**"I know what is coming, nothing that arrives is a surprise, and I am carrying none of it in my head."**

Two failure modes, pulling opposite ways — the same structure as `goal/todo.md`'s, and the reason that document's tension was the substance of its problem:

- **Blindness** — something arrives that should have been seen coming. Guarded by H2 (the record is complete), H5 (it fires whether or not anyone looks) and H8 (it is visible without a ritual).
- **Noise** — the horizon fills, stops being read, and blindness returns through the front door. Guarded by H4, the only mechanism here that can shorten the horizon without shortening the record.

A design that optimizes either alone fails.

## What is invented rather than derived

Two things go past the evidence and should be argued with. **The ramp-up window as a per-matter parameter** — the need for run-up is well evidenced; that this is its shape is not. And **the docket as a document kind of its own** rather than a mode of something existing, which Qb accepted deliberately and which sets a precedent for the next candidate.

*Reorient's centrality and the day's selection have left this list*: the first on the user's account of what the flow is for, the second on era 3's spontaneous practice.

## Open

**Qa. RESOLVED — the matter recurs, its tasks do not.** See H7a. What is left belongs at the keyboard: **the walk's drop gesture now has two possible meanings for a generated item** — *skip this occurrence* or *this occurrence never happened and is still owed*. MT5a rejected exactly this shape once already, on the grounds that a control which changes meaning depending on invisible state is how a UI becomes surprising, so the two have to be told apart rather than merged.

**Qb. RESOLVED — four types, and the increment is paid for rather than waived.** *"If you have three of something, you'll end up with N"* — true, and the counting rule survives that as long as the number stays a constraint rather than a defence. What is added is exactly one type: **the docket, a document kind with its own UX**, as TODO is. **The horizon is not a second addition** — compact and full, it is a *view over every instance of that type*, which is what the tag pivot and the link directory already are to TODO. And reorient spans types, so it is a flow rather than a type. **Three becomes four, not five**, and the next candidate must make the same argument this one did: why it cannot be a mode of something existing. `scope.md` is amended when this ships, not before — it describes what is built.

**Qc. Open, and to be designed deliberately** rather than defaulted to YAML. What binds it: lenient parse, precise serialize, untouched lines round-tripped byte-for-byte, degrading to something a plain reader finds sensible, and type declared by name for merge safety. **One constraint is new and comes from H3** — while editing is done on the raw file, *the file is the surface two people read together*, so it has to be legible aloud. Deep nesting reads badly; a table reads well.

**Qd. RESOLVED as scope and shape** — the three movements above. Two smaller things are left, and both are cheap:

- **Is era 3's "urgent" section the same practice as its "today" section?** H9 assumes so and merges the bands on that reading. If they were genuinely two, the merge is wrong and T9 survives separately.
- **Does the selection carry an order?** *"How I was going to structure my day"* may mean sequence, not just membership. If it does, the band is the first place in this design where a person orders things by hand, and everything else is creation order or derived.

**Qe. Where the day's selection is stored.** Not designed here, but the precedent is strong and worth naming so it is not re-derived: `walked` and `carriedFrom` live in the day's own frontmatter, on the argument that they are metadata about that precise day and not text anybody typed. A selection made by clicking is the same kind of thing — and it must not survive the carry, because a `today` mark that persists is a decision from a day that has ended.

## Decisions and requirements this revisits

- **R19 is promoted**, against the evidence its own gate demanded. What it got right survives: the full horizon is a plain date-ordered list, not a calendar view.
- **T11 is superseded by H11.** Same ritual, wrong scope.
- **T9's due-soon band is superseded by H9**, conditional on Qd's first question.
- **T12 and MT5c — the soft cap — are deferred, and the deferral is free.** `milestones.md` already establishes why: the cap's promise existed only because a cap degrades visibility, so with no cap there is nothing unsafe, only a longer list. What is new is that **reorient is now the evidence source** — a daily selection is a much better instrument for what the working view should hold than a number chosen in advance.
- **The single-user constraint is confirmed, and cheaply.** Two people, one screen. Recorded because the question was live and the answer forecloses a large branch.
- **`goal/todo.md`'s ban on items referencing each other is narrowly breached** by H7's completion-relative recurrence and by *"schedule the SA-512 maintenance after the normal service."* The ban rests on twenty years of evidence that general cross-reference is low value; what is needed is only *completion of X advances Y*, which does not reopen the general case.
- **`scope.md`'s counting rule goes to four** — see Qb, and amend when built.

## D68: R19 is promoted, and the fourth view type is the docket

**Date:** 2026-09-10
**Status:** decided
**Supersedes:** R19. **Amends:** `goal/scope.md`'s counting rule, T9, T11.
**Design:** `goal/horizon.md`.

**Decision.** The events calendar becomes a feature. The document kind is a
**docket** — a complete, durable set of standing commitments in one domain,
edited as a group. One thing on it is a **matter**. The **horizon** is the view
over every docket, compact and full. **Reorient** is the flow that spans them.

**Why the gate opened.** R19 held this to a pinned markdown file and demanded a
recorded failure before anything more. R18 shipped months ago, a table could have
been made on any day since, and it was not. This project's own rule is that *a
gate that was never opened has not returned a negative* — this one was opened,
and it did. What a plain file lacks is not storage: it does not order itself,
does not retire what has passed, does not reach the task list, and nothing shows
it to you, so it is not maintained. **The surfacing is the feature.** Identical
in shape to what T9 found about due dates, where era 2 stored them and missed
them anyway.

**The counting rule goes to three-plus-one, and the increment is paid for.**
Exactly one type is added. The horizon is *not* a second one — it is a view over
every instance of the type, which is what the tag pivot and the link directory
already are to TODO — and reorient is a flow, not a type. The rule survives
because the number is still a constraint: **the next candidate must argue why it
cannot be a mode of something existing.** `scope.md` is amended when this ships.

**Names chosen against a specific failure**, not for taste. "Schedule" and
"event" each burn a word needed one layer down — every matter *has* a recurrence
schedule, and "event" must stay usable as an ordinary word. "Item" belongs to
TODO and "entry" to filesets, which is why the inner noun is neither.

**What would reopen this.** The docket proving to be a mode of the TODO surface
after all, which would return the count to three.

## D69: Tephra reads calendars from files and never writes to one

**Date:** 2026-09-10
**Status:** decided
**Design:** `goal/horizon.md` H12.

**Decision.** Dated rows may be read from an **ICS file kept in the notebook**.
Tephra does not write to Google Calendar or any external service, and trips
continue to be entered there by hand.

**Why.** Both directions were implied by the source notes, and they cost
radically different things. Reading an ICS file costs a parser; the file is a
file, so R25 (full function offline), R26 (plain durable formats) and the
"program over a directory" premise are untouched. Writing costs OAuth, tokens, a
network dependency and the first service this app has ever talked to — and
`notes.md` already distinguishes the kinds of dependency worth taking. The user's
own judgement settled it: *"I'd rather manage trips separately and manually add
them than do major feature bloat just to support that."*

**What would reopen this.** Manual entry of trip calendar items proving frequent
and irritating enough to outweigh a service dependency. Note that the read
direction landing first makes this cheaper to revisit, not harder.

## D70: Two people, one screen — the single-user constraint holds

**Date:** 2026-09-10
**Status:** decided
**Confirms:** the "single user, no multi-tenancy, no sharing model" constraint in
`goal/requirements.md`.

**Decision.** The household docket is worked on jointly, and that requires
**no sharing model.** The need is two people in one room reading one screen, not
two people with accounts. *"Who owns what"* is a column, not an identity.

**Why this needed deciding rather than assuming.** Two of this project's hottest
wants turned out to be shared surfaces — the household docket, and era 3's
events spreadsheet, which was co-owned with an exec assistant and functioned as
*"a communication channel with someone who helped me plan and manage things."*
Against a constraint reading "single user," that is the kind of thing that
quietly grows into sync, identity and permissions. Asking the cheap question
first — **access, or in the room?** — collapsed it to a legibility requirement:
the docket view must be readable at conversational distance and navigable while
talking. In this project legibility requirements are hard requirements, so this
is a real obligation and a very small one.

**Same shape as D46**, where moving a boundary out to a coarser container deleted
the propagation entirely rather than resolving it.

**What would reopen this.** Wanting the other person to edit when not in the
room, which is a different product and should be recognised as one.

That's a better cut than mine, and I think it's better for a reason worth naming: my version distinguished two kinds of member *inside* one region by a mark, which is precisely the shape MT5a rejected — a region that means two things depending on what put something there.

Your line is **volition versus imposition**, and the consequence is the interesting part: *a due date approaching has more in common with a talk approaching than with anything you chose.* Both are the world bearing down. So the compact horizon isn't "upcoming events" — it's **everything approaching, whatever its source**, which is what the name meant all along. The horizon is defined by distance, not by kind.

And it makes T9 *stronger*, not just tidier. A due-soon band above the task list only fires when you're already looking at the task list — but the way a deadline gets missed is by not looking. The horizon strip is present while you're writing.

It also dissolves an objection I raised two turns ago and got wrong. I rejected "due-soon as advice at the moment of choosing" because a date arriving Wednesday would never be seen unless you chose to reorient Wednesday. That only held while the horizon was reorient-only. With an always-present strip, the strip is lapse-proof and reorient is where it *informs a decision*.
Recorded, including an amendment to D68 — the merge was wrong within the same day it was written, and the *reason* it was tempting (two stacked bands are era 2's "scan two ways at once" failure) will recur, so it's worth having the answer written down: there's only ever one band on the list, and the other thing lives somewhere else entirely.

**What this changed beyond the band.** The horizon is no longer "a view over dockets" — it's a **query over everything dated**, spanning dockets and the task list both. That's D9's filtered-view pattern, corpus-wide, exactly the shape the link directory already took. Which incidentally makes Qb's answer sturdier than when I wrote it: the horizon was already not a type, and now it's obviously not one.

Two small things fell out that I recorded as working answers rather than open questions:

- **The horizon runs from a little behind you to some distance ahead.** Something overdue is as much a thing to have in mind as something coming, so the strip isn't purely future-facing.
- **Qf — does a due date want its own lead time?** H4 gives every matter an authored ramp-up window, and the question transfers now that due dates feed the same surface. Working answer: **no.** Per-matter windows exist because a birthday needs months and an air filter needs days; task deadlines are short-fuse, era 1 records that dated tasks were "surprisingly small" in number, and a second parameter on `DUE` would complicate the one notation `goal/todo.md` was careful to keep single. **Still open, and both cheap:**

1. **Does the day's selection carry an order?** Unanswered from last turn, and it's the one place this design might let a person hand-order something — everything else is creation order or derived.
2. **Qc, the docket syntax.** The last real design question here.

On Qc, the constraint that's doing the most work isn't serialization at all — it's that while editing happens on the raw file, *the file is the surface you and your wife read together while talking.* That argues hard for something table-shaped and flat, and against nested YAML, which reads badly aloud.
